readings.unit: Complete JEP 444, Virtual Threads
readings.revision: JEP 444; official OpenJDK page; published Thu, 04 Jun 2026 17:38:09 GMT (Jina header timestamp, not verified as original publication date); retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 435 lines (1-435); Summary, History, Goals, Non-Goals, Motivation (4 subsections), Description including all Detailed changes (9 API areas), Alternatives, Testing, Risks and Assumptions, Dependencies; both code examples; one linked thread-dump screenshot was not rendered or inspected
readings.omissions: Linked JEPs, APIs, implementation code and tests not read; no execution.
sections: Motivation > Improving scalability with the asynchronous style
Motivation > Preserving the thread-per-request style with virtual threads
Description > Using virtual threads vs. platform threads
Description > Do not pool virtual threads
Description > Memory use and interaction with garbage collection
Detailed changes > Debugging (JVM TI, JDWP, JDI)
notes: Source claim: the three goals are throughput for thread-per-request servers at near-optimal hardware use, adoption through the existing java.lang.Thread API with minimal change, and troubleshooting with existing JDK tools; the non-goals explicitly exclude removing platform threads, changing Java's concurrency model, and adding a data-parallelism construct.

Source claim: the definition is contrastive - a virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread not tied to one OS thread, scheduled M:N onto carriers, versus platform threads (1:1) and early Java green threads (M:1); the scheduler is a work-stealing ForkJoinPool in FIFO mode whose parallelism defaults to availableProcessors and which is distinct from the LIFO common pool.

Source claim: most JDK blocking operations unmount the virtual thread; a few (notably filesystem operations and Object.wait) block the carrier, and their implementations temporarily expand scheduler parallelism up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize. Pinning, by contrast, is explicitly not compensated by parallelism expansion.

Source claim: JDK 21 pinning has exactly two stated causes - executing inside a synchronized block or method, or executing a native method or foreign function - and the JEP states pinning threatens scalability, not correctness.

Source claim: migration diagnostics are three distinct mechanisms - the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event (enabled by default, 20ms threshold), jdk.tracePinnedThreads with full/short modes, and jdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals for thread-local removal.

Source claim: the compatibility surface is wider than pinning - Thread.getAllStackTraces() is narrowed to platform threads, blocking Socket/ServerSocket/DatagramSocket I/O becomes interruptible (interrupt unparks and closes the socket), setDaemon and setPriority become no-ops, getThreadGroup returns a placeholder VirtualThreads group, SecurityManager gives no permissions, ThreadMXBean stays platform-only, and JVM TI GetAllThreads/GetAllStackTraces exclude virtual threads.

Source claim: the source and binary risks are enumerated narrowly - new Thread methods and the nested Thread.Builder interface can break subclasses at compile time, and the new final isVirtual() can raise IncompatibleClassChangeError if a compiled subclass declares a same-signature method.

Source claim: stacks live in the heap as growable stack-chunk objects, are not GC roots, and G1 does not support humongous stack chunks, so a stack reaching half a region (possibly as small as 512KB) may throw StackOverflowError - a per-thread stack limit, not a thread-count limit.

Source claim: observability is deliberately split rather than extended - jstack-style dumps are not widened to virtual threads; a new jcmd Thread.dump_to_file dump (text or JSON) groups threads, omits object addresses, locks, JNI and heap statistics, and does not pause the application; with jdk.trackAllThreads=false some builder-created threads may be absent from it.

Inference, not source claim: the illustrative figures (200 platform-pool tasks/s versus about 10,000 or 1,000,000 tasks/s) are presented as expected scale after warmup, with no measurement method or result table, so they must not be cited as benchmark evidence; likewise the 2026-06-04 header timestamp postdates the JDK 21 finalization the body describes and is best read as a page-served timestamp.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Its scope note says only named JEP 444 sections were inspected; this full-body read can now support the scheduler and pinning paragraphs from Scheduling virtual threads and Executing virtual threads, and the not-performed list can drop full JEP 491 body inspection once R016 is accepted.

The page treats pinning as the main release-dependent difference; the JEP adds behavioral differences that change migration advice independently - getAllStackTraces() narrowed to platform threads, blocking socket I/O becoming interruptible and closing the socket, setDaemon/setPriority no-ops, placeholder VirtualThreads group, and ThreadMXBean/JVM TI platform-only views.

The JEP separates two arguments that pooling advice often merges - virtual threads are too cheap to pool, and concurrency limits belong in constructs such as semaphores; check the page keeps no-pooling distinct from no-admission-control and leaves connection budgets to the connection-pool page.

Cancellation ownership can cite the JEP's stated side effect: interrupting a virtual thread blocked on Socket, ServerSocket or DatagramSocket unparks it and closes the socket, so interruption is not a neutral stop signal for a connection.

readings.unit: Complete JEP 491, Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
readings.revision: JEP 491; official OpenJDK page; no Published Time field present in the retrieved representation, so no publication date is asserted; retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 128 lines (1-128); Summary, Goals, Motivation (4 subsections), Description (3 subsections), Future Work, Alternatives, Risks and Assumptions, Dependencies; the single code example; this JEP has no History, Non-Goals or Testing section
readings.omissions: Linked JEPs, APIs, JVM implementation code, JVM TI specification and tests not read; no execution.
sections: Motivation > Virtual threads are pinned in synchronized methods
Description > Diagnosing remaining cases of pinning
Description > The system property jdk.tracePinnedThreads is no longer needed
Description > Choosing between synchronized and java.util.concurrent.locks
notes: Source claim: the goal is that virtual threads blocking in synchronized methods and statements release their platform threads, so existing libraries that use synchronized need no rewrite to scale; a second goal is better diagnostics for the pinning that remains.

Source claim: the cause is bookkeeping, not language design - the JVM records monitor ownership against the carrier platform thread rather than the virtual thread, so unmounting inside a monitor would let the next virtual thread mounted on that carrier appear to own the monitor and destroy mutual exclusion, which is why the JVM prevents unmounting.

Source claim: three blocking shapes are addressed - blocking to enter a monitor held elsewhere, blocking inside a synchronized region, and Object.wait()/timed wait with monitor re-acquisition after notify; each now unmounts and is resubmitted to the scheduler, possibly resuming on a different carrier.

Source claim: the alternative of expanding scheduler parallelism is rejected on scaling grounds, since the maximum platform threads available to the scheduler is limited and stated to default to 256, so no parallelism value rescues many virtual threads blocked in monitors.

Source claim: diagnostics change in both directions - jdk.tracePinnedThreads is removed and setting it has no effect (it is also described as problematic because traces printed while executing critical code), while jdk.VirtualThreadPinned is retained for native/foreign callback pinning and enhanced to convey the pin reason and the carrier identity.

Source claim: remaining pinning is enumerated as exactly three Future Work cases - blocking while resolving a symbolic reference and loading a class, blocking inside a class initializer, and waiting for another thread to finish class initialization - each attributed to a native frame or blocking in the JVM, and described as rarely problematic.

Source claim: the only stated performance risk is narrow and directional - exiting a monitor may now have to queue a virtual thread to the scheduler, which is currently less efficient than unparking a platform thread; no throughput, latency or benchmark figure is given.

Source claim: the change depends on a Java 23 JVM TI specification change to GetObjectMonitorUsage so it no longer reports monitors owned by virtual threads, justified by the bookkeeping cost of locating monitors of unmounted virtual threads; the JEP body itself names no delivering JDK release for its own feature.

Inference, not source claim: the Summary's nearly all cases of pinning is deliberately scoped by native frames, the three Future Work cases and the retained event, so any statement that JDK 24 removes pinning would overstate the text; the defensible claim is that monitor-based pinning stops being a scheduler hazard in the covered cases.

Inference, not source claim: because the retrieved representation has no status or release header, the book's JDK 24 attribution cannot be confirmed from this file and must continue to rest on the release announcements already cited in the chapter; the 128-line body is also materially shorter than JEP 444 and omits testing and non-goal sections, which limits what compatibility evidence it can supply.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Lines 84, 100 and 134 rest on the implementation review and release announcements because the canonical body was not retrievable; R016 supplies that body, so the not-fully-accessible caveat can be retired and the unmount-while-holding-a-monitor mechanism sourced to Description, while the LM_LEGACY locking-mode caveat remains implementation-review-only and should be labelled as such.

The page carries jdk.tracePinnedThreads forward as a JDK 21 diagnostic; the JEP states the property is removed and that setting it has no effect, so any JDK 24+ guidance should state the release boundary and point to the retained jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event instead.

Replace a general some-pinning-remains hedge with the JEP's exact residual set - class loading and symbolic resolution, class initializer blocking, waiting for class initialization, and native/foreign callbacks - plus the narrow monitor-exit scheduling cost as the stated performance risk.

The case is a JDK 21 monitor-pinning incident; JEP 491 changes that specific cause but not instrumentation cost or downstream capacity, so the case should keep its JDK 21 vintage explicit and must not be read as describing current releases.

notes: Source claim: every cross-process call should have connection and request timeouts; too-high timeouts retain resources, too-low timeouts cause retries and can turn small latency increases into an outage.

Source claim: a practical timeout starts from the downstream latency distribution, for example accepting 0.1% false timeouts at p99.9, with padding for tight distributions and extra allowance for internet or connection setup.
Source claim: retries are selfish and can amplify overload; a five-layer stack with three retries per layer can multiply load by 243, so retrying at one layer is preferred for low-cost operations.
Source claim: exponential backoff should be capped, but a cap makes clients retry at a constant rate; limiting retry count and returning failure earlier is preferable.
Source claim: APIs with side effects need idempotency before retries are safe; client errors generally should not be retried, though eventual consistency blurs that boundary.
Source claim: jitter spreads correlated retries and periodic work; deterministic per-host jitter preserves reproducibility for diagnosis, while random jitter hides patterns.
Inference: the 0.1%/p99.9 choice is a policy trade-off, not a universal timeout formula; the article gives no adaptive control law.
Inference: the article is first-party operational guidance, not a controlled experiment; the 243x multiplication is arithmetic, not a measured incident.

readings.coverage: All 460 lines / 11878 words; sections Motivation, Persistence, Efficiency, Producer, Consumer, Replication, Log Compaction, Quotas; diagrams not visually inspected
readings.omissions: Linked papers, code and implementation behavior not read or executed; no benchmark or independent verification.
notes: Source claim: Kafka stores messages in a persistent log, relies on the filesystem pagecache for caching, and uses sequential reads/writes rather than per-consumer B-trees.
Source claim: batching, a shared binary message format and sendfile zero-copy reduce small I/O and byte copies; TLS disables the sendfile path.
Source claim: producers choose partitions by key hash or random assignment; asynchronous batching trades a small latency bound for throughput.
Source claim: consumers pull and control their offset, so a slow consumer falls behind rather than being pushed into overload.
Source claim: replication is per partition with a leader and followers; an in-sync replica set (ISR) is maintained, and a write is committed only after all ISR members receive it.
Source claim: acks=0/1/all and min.insync.replicas define the durability/availability trade-off; the no-loss guarantee holds only while at least one ISR replica stays alive.
Source claim: unclean leader election can restore availability at the cost of losing committed messages; log compaction retains the last value per key and preserves offsets.
Source claim: client quotas limit per-broker bandwidth or request-thread time and throttle violators by delaying responses and muting channels.
Inference: the document describes mechanisms and trade-offs, not measured throughput; the 4.1 docs are explicitly older than 4.3.
Inference: "committed" means all current ISR replicas, not all assigned replicas; a shrinking ISR weakens the durability claim.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the partition page distinguish ISR commit from all assigned replicas and from producer acks?
Does the acknowledgment page keep acks, min.insync.replicas and unclean election as separate choices?
Does the offsets page distinguish log compaction offset stability from consumer position?

readings.unit: Complete document: pgvector README
readings.revision: Rolling master README; installation example pins v0.8.7; retrieved 2026-10-24; no commit hash pinned
readings.coverage: All 1366 lines / 5394 words; sections Installation, Storing, Querying, Indexing, HNSW, IVFFlat, Filtering, Multitenancy, Iterative Scans, Quantization, Sparse/Hybrid, Performance, Scaling, Monitoring, Reference, Installation Notes, Upgrading
readings.omissions: Linked examples, code and implementation behavior not read or executed; no benchmark or independent verification.
notes: Source claim: pgvector is a Postgres extension for exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search over dense, half-precision, binary and sparse vectors, using L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming or Jaccard distance.
Source claim: without an index the search is exact; an HNSW or IVFFlat index trades recall for speed and can change query results.
Source claim: HNSW uses a multilayer graph with m and ef_construction build options and ef_search query option; IVFFlat uses lists and probes and should be built after data exists.
Source claim: with approximate indexes, filters are applied after the index scan, so a restrictive filter can return fewer rows; iterative scans, partial indexes and partitioning are mitigations.
Source claim: multitenancy should use partitioning or separate tables because a shared approximate index lets one tenant affect another tenant's recall and speed.
Source claim: binary/half-precision quantization and subvector indexing reduce working-set size, with re-ranking for recall; indexes need not fit in memory but usually perform better when they do.
Source claim: pgvector uses WAL, so replication and point-in-time recovery apply; vector dimensions and index types have documented limits.
Inference: the README is usage documentation, not a benchmark; recall and latency depend on data, parameters and workload.
Inference: filtering-after-scan is both a recall issue and an authorization-boundary issue; the docs describe mechanics, not an access-control guarantee.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the filtering page treat post-index filtering as both a recall and an authorization boundary?
Does the engine page keep documentation claims separate from measured recall and latency?
Does the architecture page treat index build, memory and WAL as operational constraints?

readings.unit: Complete document: OpenTelemetry Metrics Data Model
readings.revision: OpenTelemetry specification page; status mixed/stable sections; retrieved 2026-10-24; no page revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 804 lines / 8395 words; sections Overview, Events => Data Stream => Timeseries, Model Details, Metric Points, Exemplars, Data point flags, Single-Writer, Temporality, Resets and Gaps, Overlap, Stream Manipulations; diagrams not visually inspected
readings.omissions: Linked guides, code and implementation behavior not read or executed; no benchmark or independent verification.
notes: Source claim: the model separates the event, timeseries and OTLP stream layers, and every OTLP stream has a decomposable aggregate function so temporal and spatial reaggregation is semantically defined.

Source claim: metric identity is resource, scope, name and identifying data-point properties; description is not identifying, while histogram bucket boundaries and exponential-histogram scale are extrinsic.
Source claim: point kinds are Sum, Gauge, Histogram and ExponentialHistogram; a monotonic Sum maps to a Counter, a non-monotonic Sum to a Gauge, and Summary is legacy.
Source claim: Sum, Histogram and ExponentialHistogram support delta or cumulative temporality; StartTimeUnixNano is strongly recommended to interpret rates and resets.
Source claim: the single-writer principle requires one logical writer per stream; overlapping or duplicate writers are an error state, and receivers should deduplicate or surface the conflict.
Source claim: resets and gaps are encoded through timestamps; cumulative streams with unknown start time can overcount rate if the first point is lost.
Source claim: delta-to-cumulative conversion is stateful and must reach one destination; alignment gaps or overlaps trigger reset or deduplication decisions.
Inference: the spec defines transport semantics, not a guarantee that a backend preserves them after ingestion or query.
Inference: single-writer and temporality choices are correctness constraints, not merely collector configuration.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the metric-semantics page keep units, temporality, reset handling and single-writer identity as separate conditions?
Does the cardinality page distinguish identity attributes from non-identifying description or bucket metadata?
Does the SLO page avoid treating a backend aggregation as semantically equivalent to the OTLP stream?

readings.unit: Complete document: RabbitMQ Reliability Guide
readings.revision: Rolling RabbitMQ documentation; retrieved 2026-10-24; no page revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 124 lines / 1994 words; sections Overview, What Can Fail?, Connection Failures, Acknowledgements and Confirms, Heartbeats, Data Safety on the RabbitMQ Side, Clustering and Queue Content Replication, Data Safety on the Publisher Side, Data Safety on the Consumer Side, Unprocessable Deliveries, Consumer Cancel Notification, Federation and Shovel, Monitoring and Health Checks; diagrams not visually inspected
readings.omissions: Linked guides, code and implementation behavior not read or executed; no benchmark or independent verification.
sections: Data Safety on the RabbitMQ Side
Data Safety on the Publisher Side
Data Safety on the Consumer Side
notes: Source claim: reliable delivery is a joint responsibility of brokers, publishers and consumers; network failures, node crashes and application errors are all in scope.
Source claim: acknowledgements and publisher confirms signal receipt and transfer of ownership, not merely TCP delivery; without them the guarantee is at-most-once, with them at-least-once.
Source claim: durable queues and persistent messages are required for broker-side restart safety; quorum queues and streams replicate queue state with a leader and followers.
Source claim: a publisher that does not receive a confirm may retransmit, so duplicates are possible and consumers must deduplicate or be idempotent.
Source claim: redelivery sets a redelivered flag, but the absence of the flag guarantees only that the message was not seen before; rejected messages can be requeued or dead-lettered.
Source claim: heartbeats detect dead TCP connections; monitoring and health checks cover slower failures, with false positives if checks are excessive.
Inference: the guide describes mechanisms and contracts, not a measured delivery guarantee for a specific deployment.
Inference: at-least-once plus retry makes consumer idempotency or dedup a correctness requirement, not an optimization.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the messaging page separate broker acknowledgement from the consumer durable effect?
Does the workflow page treat redelivery and duplicate effects as expected failure modes?
Does the selection page distinguish retention, replication and consumer acknowledgement?

readings.unit: Complete document: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
readings.revision: RFC 9700, January 2025; retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 1091 lines / 16221 words; Abstract through Security Considerations, References and Acknowledgements; sections 1-7; diagrams/code examples read as text
readings.omissions: Normative references and linked specifications not read in full; no implementation or test execution.
notes: Source claim: the BCP updates OAuth 2.0 security guidance for redirect-based flows, token replay, privilege restriction, client authentication and the resource-owner password grant.
Source claim: authorization servers should use exact redirect URI matching; wildcard/pattern matching and open redirectors enable code and token leakage.
Source claim: public clients must use PKCE; PKCE also protects against authorization code injection, and a server must reject a code_verifier when no code_challenge was sent.
Source claim: mix-up attacks require a client that interacts with multiple authorization servers to bind the issuer to the user-agent session and verify the issuer or use distinct redirect URIs.
Source claim: access tokens should be sender-constrained and audience-restricted; refresh tokens for public clients need rotation or sender constraint, with revocation on replay.
Source claim: the HTTP 307 redirect can expose credentials in a POST body; authorization servers must not use 307 for requests carrying credentials and should prefer 303.
Source claim: reverse proxies must sanitize security-relevant headers, and in-browser postMessage flows require exact origin matching and no wildcard receiver.
Inference: the BCP is normative guidance, not a claim that any deployment implements every recommendation.
Inference: several mitigations are conditional on client type, deployment model and protocol version; a checklist without those conditions is insufficient.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the credential page separate token validity, audience, sender constraint and revocation?
Does the security-test page include cross-resource token reuse and PKCE downgrade tests?
Does the identity page distinguish authentication, authorization and token replay?

readings.unit: Complete paper: Statistical Analysis with Little's Law
readings.revision: Operations Research 61(4), 2013, pp. 1030-1045; DOI 10.1287/opre.2013.1193; retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 1235 lines / 15334 words; sections 1-7, theorems, tables and references; formulas read as text
readings.omissions: Supplemental e-companion, referenced papers and data archive not read; no reanalysis or simulation executed.
sections: 2. Measurement Over a Finite Time Interval
6. Confidence Intervals for the Refined Estimator
notes: Source claim: L = lambda W is well founded for long-run averages and stationary expected values, but measurements over a finite interval are neither; the equality holds only when the system starts and ends empty.
Source claim: the extended finite-time law expresses the bias as edge-effect areas from customers present before time 0 and after time t; the exact relation is not a simple equality.
Source claim: altering definitions to an inside view forces equality but censors waiting time and makes batch-means confidence intervals problematic.
Source claim: the paper advocates a statistical approach, using batch means for a single stationary segment and independent replications across days for nonstationary service systems.
Source claim: the estimator L/lambda is biased when waiting times are not observed; the bias depends on the model and can be reduced with a refined estimator using initial and terminal counts.
Source claim: a call-center example shows confidence intervals, stationarity checks and bias reduction change the interpretation of finite measurements.
Source claim: infinite-server and single-server models have different bias behavior; a refinement that works for many-server systems can fail for a single-server queue.
Inference: the paper is about estimation from finite data, not a claim that Little's Law predicts tail latency or chooses capacity.
Inference: a page that treats L = lambda W as a direct equality on any observed interval would overstate the theorem.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the page keep the finite-interval edge effects and the mean-only scope of Little's Law explicit?
Does the measurement page avoid treating an observed interval average as an unbiased estimate of W?
Does the tail page avoid using Little's Law to predict a percentile?

Also omitted from reading: link targets and anchor URLs stripped by the reader normalizer; linked specifications (RFC 9111 Caching, 9112 HTTP/1.1, 9113 HTTP/2, 9114 HTTP/3, 3986 URI, 5234 ABNF, 6125, 7616/7617, 6265 Cookie, 8941) not read; no implementation, server, proxy or benchmark execution.
sections: 1 Introduction (1.1 Purpose, 1.2 History and Evolution, 1.3 Core Semantics, 1.4 Specifications Obsoleted)
2 Conformance (2.1 Syntax Notation, 2.2 Requirements Notation, 2.3 Length Requirements, 2.4 Error Handling, 2.5 Protocol Version)
Appendix B Changes from Previous RFCs (B.2-B.5, B.9)
notes: Source claim (2.2, 2.5): conformance is scoped to the roles an implementation plays and to the messaging syntax version in use, while core semantics are shared across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Inference: any Tycho statement of the form 'HTTP requires X' is under-specified unless it names the role (client, origin, proxy, cache) and the version; benchmark results cannot be generalized from one role to another.

Source claim (9.2.1-9.2.2): safety and idempotency describe the effect the client requested, not server-side logging, revision history or other incidental side effects; PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are idempotent, POST is not. Inference: retry experiments must define the observable intended effect and the failure window (before or after the response), because a method name alone does not establish that a replay is safe.

Source claim (9.2.2): a proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests, a client SHOULD NOT retry a failed automatic retry, and clients may guess retryability after connection loss before any response part arrives. Inference: duplicate-work measurements need attempt provenance (client, proxy, gateway) and the exact failure point; otherwise duplicated load is attributed to the server or to the method rather than to a retry policy.

Source claim (8.6, 5.3, 7.6.1): Content-Length must match the actual framing, duplicate identical values may be collapsed, inconsistent values risk request smuggling, and hop-by-hop fields listed in Connection must be removed by intermediaries. Inference: framing validity and intermediary stripping are preconditions for interpreting throughput or error-rate results; a benchmark that tolerates malformed framing measures a different system than the protocol describes.

Source claim (12.5.5): Vary expands the cache key, a proxy MUST NOT generate '*', and a response with Vary must not satisfy a later request with different selecting-field values. Inference: cache hit ratio is a property of the request population and Vary, not of the origin alone; Tycho cache claims should report Vary and the request mix rather than a single hit percentage.

Source claim (8.8.1, 13.1.1-13.1.2, 13.2.2): strong comparison is mandatory for If-Match and weak comparison for If-None-Match; preconditions are evaluated in a fixed order (If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Range) and only when the unconditional response would be 2xx or 412. Inference: 304 versus 412 outcomes depend jointly on validator strength and evaluation order, so conditional-request benchmarks that conflate them cannot separate cache validation from lost-update protection.

Source claim (14.2, 14.4, 17.15): Range is optional and may be ignored, satisfiable byte ranges yield 206 with Content-Range, unsatisfiable sets yield 416, overlapping or many small ranges are a denial-of-service vector, and 206 parts may be coalesced or reordered. Inference: partial-content throughput depends on server coalescing policy and client range pattern; a single 'range support' boolean is not a meaningful conformance or performance claim.

Source claim (15.5.20): a 421 Misdirected Request may be retried by a client even when the method is not idempotent, and a proxy MUST NOT generate 421. Inference: this is an explicit exception to retry conservatism and a plausible source of retry amplification in multi-origin connection reuse; Tycho retry cases should state whether 421 handling is in scope.

Source claim (15.6.4, 10.2.3): 503 indicates temporary overload or maintenance and MAY carry Retry-After as either an HTTP-date or delay-seconds; 3xx responses may also carry Retry-After as a minimum wait. Inference: neither field obliges the client to wait, so 'overload protection' claims must measure client compliance and queueing behavior, not treat Retry-After as a scheduling contract.

Source claim (11.3-11.5): authentication is a stateless challenge-response framework; a protection space is the origin plus the realm value, and credentials may be reused across requests in that space. Inference: credential-reuse tests must scope by origin and realm (including multiple challenges with the same scheme), not by hostname string; scope errors inflate apparent authentication reuse or leakage.

Version-sensitive points (5.1, 2.5, 7.8, 9.3.6, 15.2): field semantics do not change between minor versions of a major version, extension points are version-independent, but HTTP/1.0 clients must not receive 1xx and must ignore Upgrade; CONNECT uses authority-form and forbids Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding in 2xx. Inference: Tycho should tag HTTP claims with the version whose wire behavior is being described, because several statements here are explicitly version-conditioned.

Representation fidelity: the local Markdown omits 14 TOC-listed (sub)sections, including 3.7 Intermediaries, 6.3 Header Fields, 6.6/6.6.1/6.6.2 Date and Trailer metadata, 8.2/8.3.1/8.5.1 representation metadata and media type, and 17.2 intermediary risk. Inference: conclusions about proxy/gateway roles, Date semantics, header-section processing or media-type parsing cannot be sourced from this file alone and require the authoritative RFC before being used in the book.
Supplemental sections were read from the official RFC 9110 text on 2026-10-24; the record now covers all TOC sections, with the local representation gap labelled.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Method safety/idempotency and status-code classes as contract terms; separate semantics from HTTP/1.1 wire behavior when describing API compatibility.
Retry eligibility grounded in 9.2.2 (proxy MUST NOT retry non-idempotent; no retry of a failed retry) and the 421 exception in 15.5.20; require attempt provenance in retry measurements.
Validator strength and comparison functions (8.8.1, 13.1.1-13.1.2), Vary as cache-key expansion (12.5.5), and 304 header requirements (15.4.5) as acceptance criteria for cache layers.
Distinguish protocol-level idempotency (intended effect, 9.2.2) from storage-level exactly-once claims; state which failure window and which actor (client, proxy, gateway) is covered.

sections: 3.2 Updating Stored Header Fields (heading absent; body read)
4.1 Calculating Cache Keys with the Vary Header Field
notes: Source claim: section 3 makes storage conditional on conjunctive requirements -- understood method, final status, understood 206/304 or must-understand, no no-store, shared-cache private and Authorization rules, and at least one cacheability signal; a cache extension can override them (lines 242-266).

Source claim: section 3.1 requires storing all received header fields including unrecognized ones, excepts Connection-nominated, proxy-specific and no-cache/private-named fields, and says trailers may be stored separately or discarded but MUST NOT be merged with headers.

Source claim: section 3.3 permits storing an incomplete 200 or a 206 as incomplete only when Range and Content-Range are understood, the response is marked incomplete, and reuse waits until completion or a wholly contained range request.

Source claim: section 4 lists reuse preconditions (target URI, method, Vary-nominated fields, no unvalidated no-cache, and fresh, stale-permitted or validated) and requires generating Age whenever a stored response is served without validation.

Source claim: section 4.2 defines freshness as freshness_lifetime > current_age; section 4.2.1 orders lifetime sources as s-maxage for shared caches, then max-age, then Expires minus Date, then heuristic, and prefers the first occurrence or stale on duplicates and the most restrictive directive on conflict.

Source claim: section 4.2.2 forbids heuristics when an explicit expiration exists, limits them to heuristically cacheable or explicitly cacheable responses, and only encourages a heuristic value near 10 percent of the Last-Modified interval.
Source claim: section 4.2.3 computes current_age from apparent_age or corrected_age_value plus resident time; a cache without a clock MUST revalidate stored responses on every use (section 4).

Source claim: section 4.3 validation uses ETag and Last-Modified preconditions; a 304 updates identified stored responses, a full response replaces them, and a 5xx during validation may be forwarded or treated as failure with stale service or retry.

Source claim: section 4.4 requires invalidating the target URI after a non-error response to an unsafe method, permits but does not require invalidating Location and Content-Location URIs, and forbids cross-origin invalidation.

Source claim (supplemental 5.2): directives are unidirectional and proxies must pass them through; request directives are advisory while response directives in 5.2.2 must be obeyed; 5.2.2.2 must-revalidate forbids stale reuse even when disconnected and calls for an error, and 5.2.2.10 s-maxage overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches with proxy-revalidate semantics.

Source claim (supplemental 5.3-5.5): invalid Expires values including 0 mean already expired, max-age makes Expires ignored, Pragma is deprecated, and Warning is obsoleted; the 5.2.2.7 note says private controls storage location, not message privacy.

Inference: these are protocol conditions on storing and reusing a response, not evidence of hit rate, latency, origin protection or measured cache effectiveness; such claims need separate measurement, and the local file alone could not support any section 5 directive claim.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the edge-cache page keep freshness lifetime, age and validation separate from revocation and access visibility, rather than treating a TTL as an authorization boundary?
Does the cache acceptance page treat HTTP directives as constraints on reuse rather than guarantees of origin protection, hit rate or latency?
Does the stampede page distinguish request collapsing (section 4) from an origin admission budget, which RFC 9111 does not specify?

sections: 8.2.3 Compressing the Cookie Header Field (supplemental official text)
8.6 The Upgrade Header Field (body read; heading absent)
notes: Source claim: section 5 defines a stream as an independent bidirectional frame sequence; client-initiated streams use odd identifiers, server-initiated even, identifier zero is connection control, and identifiers increase monotonically and are never reused (5, 5.1.1).

Source claim: section 5.1 defines idle, reserved (local/remote), open, half-closed (local/remote) and closed states; frames not expressly permitted are connection errors by default, PRIORITY may appear in any state, and unknown extension frames cannot be judged (5.1).

Source claim: section 5.1.2 counts open and half-closed streams against SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS but excludes reserved streams; exceeding the peer limit is a stream error of PROTOCOL_ERROR or REFUSED_STREAM, and REFUSED_STREAM signals that automatic retry is intended.

Source claim: section 5.2 flow control is per-hop and credit-based through WINDOW_UPDATE, starts at 65,535 octets for each stream and the connection, applies only to DATA frames, and is controlled by the receiver while the sender must respect advertised limits.

Source claim: sections 5.2.2-5.2.3 say a maximum 2^31-1 window with prompt WINDOW_UPDATE effectively disables flow control, endpoints MUST read frames promptly or risk deadlock on critical frames, and window sizing must account for the bandwidth-delay product.

Source claim: section 5.3 deprecates RFC 7540 priority signaling, retains the frame fields and mandatory handling for interoperability, and encourages an alternative scheme such as RFC 9218 where priority signaling matters.

Source claim: section 6.8 GOAWAY carries a last-stream-ID and error code; receivers MUST NOT open new streams, streams above the boundary are treated as unprocessed and may be retried on a new connection, and a sender MUST NOT increase the last-stream-ID across successive GOAWAY frames.

Source claim: section 6.8 recommends an initial GOAWAY with last-stream-ID 2^31-1 and NO_ERROR, a wait of at least one round trip, then a second GOAWAY with the updated boundary; after GOAWAY, HEADERS, PUSH_PROMISE and CONTINUATION must be minimally processed for HPACK consistency and DATA must count toward connection flow control.

Source claim: section 8.1 frames a message as HEADERS plus CONTINUATION, zero or more DATA, and optional trailer HEADERS; content-length mismatch, pseudo-headers in trailers, and a post-final HEADERS frame without END_STREAM make a message malformed, and intermediaries must not forward malformed messages.

Source claim (supplemental 8.2): field names must be lowercase; 8.2.1 mandates minimal validation of names and values to prevent request smuggling; 8.2.2 forbids connection-specific header fields including Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding and Upgrade, with TE: trailers as the only exception.

Source claim (supplemental 8.3): pseudo-headers must precede regular fields, must not repeat or cross request/response context, and requests require :method, :scheme and :path while responses require :status; 8.7 ties GOAWAY and REFUSED_STREAM to safe automatic retry of unprocessed requests.

Inference: the GOAWAY boundary is a per-hop statement that a stream might have been processed, not an application rollback; retry safety above the boundary is a transport claim, while flow-control windows bound bytes in transit rather than application demand or durable buffering.

Does the balancing page distinguish connection-level selection from per-stream concurrency, given that one multiplexed connection can carry most requests while peers carry one each?
Does the streaming page separate HTTP/2 transport flow-control windows from application demand, backpressure and durable replay?

Source claim: compaction produces blocks spanning up to 10% of retention or 31 days, whichever is smaller; source and compacted blocks coexist so disk can briefly exceed `storage.tsdb.retention.size`. Inference: the configured size limit is not a hard instantaneous disk ceiling.

Source claim: recording-rule backfill limitations include duplicate blocks on repeated overlapping runs, evaluation of all rules, rule `interval` overriding `--eval-interval`, ignored alerts, and no visibility of earlier rules in the same group. notes: Source claim: multipart upload splits one object into contiguous parts that can be uploaded independently and in any order, and a failed part can be retransmitted without affecting others. Inference: 'any order' describes transfer scheduling; completion still concatenates parts by ascending part number, so receive order is not object order.

Source claim: AWS recommends multipart upload for objects 100 MB or larger and lists throughput, recovery, pause/resume and unknown-final-size benefits. Inference: these are general recommendations, not service limits or a universal part-size choice; the page defers limits to a separate linked page.

Source claim: initiation returns an upload ID; part numbers range from 1 to 10,000; reusing a part number overwrites the prior part; and completion concatenates parts in ascending part-number order. Inference: the client must persist per-part receipts because the source explicitly says the listing is not authoritative for completion.

Source claim: when checksums are used, part numbers must be consecutive and begin at 1, and nonconsecutive numbers cause an HTTP 500 error. Inference: the earlier allowance for nonconsecutive part numbers is conditional, so checksum choice changes a protocol constraint that belongs in the upload state model.

Source claim: a completed multipart object's ETag is not necessarily an MD5 hash of its bytes, and full-object checksum validation can fail with BadDigest. Inference: ETag equality alone is not end-to-end content verification or a portable content digest.

Source claim: an initiated upload has no expiry; uncompleted parts are retained and billed until completion or abort; and aborting while part uploads are in flight does not guarantee immediate release. Inference: cleanup must coordinate quiescence and verify storage release rather than assume abort is synchronous.

Source claim: for concurrent uploads to the same key in a versioning-enabled bucket, the most recently initiated upload becomes current even if an earlier upload completes later; unversioned buckets can let another request take precedence. Inference: completion order and publication order are distinct, so application-level arbitration or a conditional write is required.

Source claim: conditional writes are available for PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload to prevent overwriting an existing key. Inference: this addresses create-if-absent or precondition races, not crash recovery, session ownership or cross-store metadata publication.

Source claim: permissions differ by operation (s3:PutObject, s3:AbortMultipartUpload, s3:ListMultipartUploadParts and s3:ListBucketMultipartUploads), and missing KMS or SSE-C material can cause completion to create an object without a checksum. Inference: technical completion does not guarantee the integrity evidence the caller expects; checksum presence needs separate verification.

Source claim: ListParts returns at most 1,000 parts per request and excludes unfinished parts, while ListMultipartUploads returns at most 1,000 uploads and is for verification only. Inference: pagination and locally persisted receipts are required for large uploads.

readings.revision: Live page; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed

notes: Source claim: cell-based architecture derives from ship bulkheads that subdivide a hull into watertight compartments. Inference: the analogy explains containment intent but does not show that software boundaries are equally watertight.

Source claim: fault-isolated boundaries restrict a failure's effect to a limited set of components, leaving components outside unaffected. Inference: 'unaffected' requires evidence that every shared dependency, routing path and operational tool sits outside the failing cell's blast radius.

Source claim: the partition key must align with the service grain and minimize cross-cell interactions, with customer ID and resource ID as examples. Inference: key selection governs hotspotting, migration cost and whether a request can be served by one cell; it is not a naming detail.

Source claim: a cell router distributes requests by partition key and presents one endpoint to clients. Inference: the router is a shared request-path dependency, so its mapping cache, staleness bound and behavior during control-plane loss need an explicit contract.

Source claim: each cell is independent, does not share state with other cells and handles a subset of workload requests. Inference: deployment separation alone does not prove state isolation; shared databases, queues, identity services, networks or control planes can violate the claim.

Source claim: with 10 cells serving 100 requests, a failure in one cell leaves 90% of requests unaffected. Inference: that arithmetic assumes even assignment, a one-cell blast radius, no shared dependency and no retry shift; it is an illustrative ratio, not a resilience guarantee.

Source claim: cells contain failures such as bad software updates and poison-pill requests. Inference: containment requires independent rollout cohorts, admission limits and bounded retries; a global deployment or shared queue can propagate the same fault.

Source claim: the architecture has a cell router, cells and a control plane that provisions, de-provisions and migrates customers; it may be zonal, regional or global; 30 hosts can remain 30 hosts. Inference: consolidation can reduce spare capacity and enlarge per-cell impact, while the control plane is both a cross-cell dependency and a privileged administrative concentration.

Source claim: a typical three-layer application serves 100% of clients and a failure or change affects 100%; the cell version partitions that workload. Inference: this is a conceptual comparison, and the source diagrams omitted from the local extract cannot be checked for topology or shared components.

Source claim: the router is described as the 'thinnest possible layer', responsible only for routing to the right cell. Inference: thin routing logic does not make the router operationally unimportant; migration still needs authoritative placement state and safe cutover rules not specified on this page.

Which dependency sets remain common across cells despite separate compute placement?

Which tenant-to-cell mapping, migration and stale-router paths can bypass tenant isolation during rebalancing?

sections: 13.3.1 Table-Level Locks and Table 13.2 Conflicting Lock Modes
13.3.2 Row-Level Locks and Table 13.3 Conflicting Row-Level Locks
notes: Source claim: explicit locking exists for application-controlled locking where MVCC does not give the desired behavior, and most commands also acquire appropriate locks automatically. Inference: lock waits can originate from ordinary SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT or MERGE even when the application never issues LOCK.

Source claim: all eight listed modes are table-level locks even where the name contains 'row'; the names are historical and conflict behavior defines the semantics. Inference: migration and capacity analysis should map each exact statement to its actual mode rather than reason from a mode's label.

Source claim: only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks SELECT without FOR UPDATE/SHARE, and ACCESS SHARE conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Inference: plain read traffic is usually insulated from index builds and weaker DDL, but not from DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER or REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW without CONCURRENTLY.

Source claim: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY acquires SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, while CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY acquires SHARE; VACUUM without FULL, ANALYZE and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY also take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE. Inference: a concurrent build removes write blocking but still conflicts with maintenance and some ALTER forms, so it is not lock-free.

Source claim: a lock is normally held until transaction end, but savepoint rollback or an error escaping a PL/pgSQL exception block releases locks acquired after that point. Inference: idle-in-transaction sessions and exception-swallowing loops have materially different lock lifetimes, so active-query duration alone is an incomplete blocker diagnostic.

Source claim: row-level locks block writers and lockers of the same row but do not affect plain data querying; SELECT FOR UPDATE marks selected rows and can therefore cause disk writes. Inference: row-lock contention appears as write and update latency plus WAL/IO cost, not as read unavailability.

Source claim: PostgreSQL detects deadlocks automatically and aborts one involved transaction, but the victim is difficult to predict and should not be relied upon; consistent multi-object lock order and acquiring the most restrictive needed lock first are recommended. Inference: application retry must restart the whole logical transaction, and external effects must be deferred until commit.

Source claim: advisory locks have session-level and transaction-level forms; session-level locks survive a rollback and require explicit unlock, transaction-level locks release at transaction end, and repeated acquisition is reentrant. Inference: session-level advisory locks conflict with naive transaction-pooling assumptions because session affinity and cleanup are application responsibilities.

Source claim: advisory and regular locks share a pool sized by max_locks_per_transaction and max_connections, and exhaustion prevents granting any locks. Inference: advisory-lock keys consume a bounded cluster-wide resource and can affect unrelated sessions, so a bounded key space and cleanup protocol are architectural requirements.

Source claim: with LIMIT, SQL evaluation order can acquire advisory locks for rows the caller never receives, leaving dangling session locks until session end. Inference: row-returning lock calls need an ordered subquery or try-lock pattern plus an explicit unlock path; a query that looks bounded can still lock unbounded rows.

Source claim: page-level share/exclusive locks are internal, released immediately after a row is fetched or updated, and application developers normally need not be concerned. Inference: page locks are not an application tuning surface and should not be blamed for user-visible lock waits without measurement.

readings.revision: PostgreSQL 17; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 280 lines / 4089 words (wc -l and wc -w match manifest); sections Synopsis, Description, Parameters, Index Storage Parameters, Building Indexes Concurrently, Notes, Examples, Compatibility; Jina Reader title/URL/published-time header, 'Markdown Content:' marker and heading permalink artifacts excluded; no navigation sidebar or cookie banner was present; no section gap.

notes: Source claim: CONCURRENTLY builds the index without taking locks that prevent concurrent inserts, updates or deletes, whereas a standard build locks out writes but not reads. Inference: the availability differentiator is write blocking; read availability is not the distinguishing property.

Source claim: a concurrent build performs two table scans and additionally waits for existing transactions that could modify or use the index, so it requires more total work and takes significantly longer. Inference: 'online' trades elapsed time, CPU, I/O and WAL for write availability; a rollout budget must reserve the longer window.

Source claim: the index is entered as invalid in one transaction, two table scans occur in two more transactions, and the build waits after the second scan for snapshots predating it, including snapshots from concurrent builds on other tables when indexes are partial or use non-simple column references. Inference: concurrent builds are not independent background jobs; old snapshots and sibling builds can serialize completion.

Source claim: even after the command completes and marks the index valid, the index may not be immediately usable while transactions exist that predate the start of the build. Inference: 'command returned' and 'planner can use it' are distinct lifecycle events and should be checked separately.

Source claim: a deadlock or uniqueness violation during a scan fails CREATE INDEX but leaves an invalid index that is ignored for querying and still consumes update overhead; the recommended recovery is to drop it and retry, or REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Inference: index existence is not evidence of a usable or cheap index; validity and cleanup need monitoring.

Source claim: for a unique concurrent index, uniqueness is enforced against other transactions once the second scan begins, so violations can surface in other queries before the index is usable, and a failure in the second scan leaves the invalid index enforcing uniqueness afterwards. Inference: failure is not a full rollback of every consequence, and 'drop and retry' can itself conflict with writes that the invalid index already rejects.

Source claim: only one concurrent index build can run on a table at a time; regular builds may run simultaneously with each other; schema modification is disallowed during the build; and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block. Inference: migration frameworks that wrap all DDL in one transaction must special-case this command, and parallel migration workers need a per-table exclusion rule.

Source claim: concurrent builds on partitioned tables are not supported, but each partition can be built concurrently and then the partitioned index created non-concurrently as a metadata-only operation. Inference: partitioned-index rollout requires per-partition scheduling plus a short parent-level lock, not a single cluster-wide concurrent command.

Source claim: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY supports parallel builds without special restrictions, but only the first table scan is actually performed in parallel. Inference: parallel speedup for the concurrent form is partial and should not be extrapolated from regular parallel builds.

Source claim: INCLUDE adds non-key columns for index-only scans, duplicates table data, can exceed the maximum index tuple size, and disables B-tree deduplication; only B-tree, GiST and SP-GiST support INCLUDE. Inference: covering indexes need size and write-amplification tests, not only a read-path argument.

Source claim: B-tree fillfactor defaults to 90, lower values can smooth page splits with workload-dependent effect, and 100 is advised only for a table certain to remain static; B-tree deduplication defaults to ON. Inference: fillfactor and deduplication are workload hypotheses to measure, not universal defaults.

Source claim: creating an index on a partitioned table recurses by default and attaches equivalent partition indexes; ONLY suppresses recursion but leaves the parent index invalid until ALTER INDEX ATTACH PARTITION, while future partitions automatically receive matching indexes. Inference: ONLY creates a deliberate intermediate state that requires a follow-up step, not a finished deployment.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the index-lifecycle page distinguish regular from concurrent builds by lock mode, scans, snapshot waits and expected elapsed time, rather than only calling the concurrent form 'not free'?
Should the forward-repair gate include a failed concurrent unique-index build that leaves an invalid index still enforcing uniqueness?
Does the DDL preflight require index-validity verification and cleanup evidence, not just lock mode and table-rewrite status?
How should the schema-evolution runbook handle CONCURRENTLY's transaction-block restriction and the per-partition staged build for partitioned tables?
Does the maintenance budget account for two scans, snapshot waits and the update overhead of an invalid index left by a failed build?

notes: Source claim: standard VACUUM makes space reusable inside existing files but returns space to the OS only when trailing pages become entirely free and an exclusive lock is easily obtained; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table, takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and needs roughly table-sized extra disk (lines 21, 29, 39).
Source claim: autovacuum never issues VACUUM FULL (line 31), so it cannot lower a table's minimum size; the page frames the goal as steady-state space use rather than minimal size.

Source claim: XIDs are 32-bit, so every table in every database must be vacuumed at least once per two billion transactions (line 79); since 9.4 freezing sets a flag bit instead of overwriting xmin (line 85). Inference: the two-billion figure is a correctness horizon, not a safe operating interval.
Source claim: vacuum_freeze_table_age is effectively capped at 0.95 x autovacuum_freeze_max_age, and the multiplier is described as deliberate room to run a manual VACUUM first (line 97).

Source claim: raising autovacuum_freeze_max_age costs about two bits of pg_xact per transaction and corresponding pg_commit_ts history - about half a gigabyte and about 20GB at two billion, about 50MB and 2GB at the 200 million default (line 99). Inference: these are documentation estimates, not measurements, and were not verified here.

Source claim: warnings begin at forty million transactions from wraparound and new XID assignment stops below three million, leaving only read-only transactions startable (lines 121-131). The page presents both margins as fixed, with no tunable named.

Source claim: the documented recovery order is prepared transactions, long-running transactions, stale replication slots, a database-wide VACUUM, then autovacuum configuration; VACUUM FULL and VACUUM FREEZE are explicitly discouraged in that state (lines 133-137).

Textual oddity: step 4 (line 136) directs vacuuming of tables where 'relminxid' is oldest, but the page elsewhere defines only relfrozenxid (lines 103, 106, 119, 170) and relminmxid (line 149); the string relminxid occurs only at line 136. Quoted as-is, likely a documentation typo; not silently corrected.

Source claim: multixact IDs and their member lists are separate 32-bit spaces in pg_multixact; aggressive scans are forced above autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age and when member storage exceeds about 10GB, with wraparound near 20GB (lines 145-151). Inference: MXID pressure is not visible through the ordinary per-table age query shown for XIDs.

Source claim: vacuum, insert-vacuum and analyze thresholds are each base plus scale factor times reltuples, and the underlying counts come from the cumulative statistics system and are eventually consistent (lines 170-186); the page gives no bound on that lag.

Source claim: partitioned tables are not processed by autovacuum while their partitions are, autovacuum issues no ANALYZE on partitioned tables, and inheritance parents are analyzed only when the parent itself changes (lines 51, 69, 188).

Source claim: a lock request conflicting with autovacuum's SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE hold interrupts it, except anti-wraparound runs, and the closing Warning says regularly running conflicting commands such as ANALYZE can prevent autovacuums from ever completing (lines 196-200). Inference: scheduling maintenance commands becomes a correctness-adjacent concern, not merely politeness.

readings.revision: PostgreSQL 17 documentation (docs/17, section 8.5); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed (the Jina wrapper's Published Time 2026-08-13 is a fetch timestamp, not a document revision)
readings.coverage: All 345 lines / 4658 words; sections 8.5 (Table 8.9), 8.5.1 with 8.5.1.1 Dates, 8.5.1.2 Times, 8.5.1.3 Time Stamps, 8.5.1.4 Special Values (Tables 8.10-8.13), 8.5.2 Date/Time Output (Tables 8.14-8.15), 8.5.3 Time Zones, 8.5.4 Interval Input (Tables 8.16-8.17), 8.5.5 Interval Output (Table 8.18); excluded from technical claims: Jina wrapper header lines 1-7 (Title, URL Source, Published Time, Markdown Content), appended heading anchors of the form [#](...), the empty-text link artefact at line 161, and collapsed table captions such as 'Table 8.9.Date/Time Types'; no cookie or navigation chrome was present in the representation

notes: Source claim (line 8): PostgreSQL supports the full SQL date/time type set and counts dates by the Gregorian calendar even in years before its introduction. Inference: this is a documented proleptic-calendar convention; this reader did not execute any calendar conversion to confirm it.

Source claim (Table 8.9, lines 12-19): fixed storage sizes (timestamp 8 bytes, date 4, timetz 12, interval 16) with 1 microsecond resolution and ranges 4713 BC to 294276 AD. Inference: the 8-byte/1us design is what bounds the upper instant, so range headroom is a physical consequence rather than a policy choice.

Source claim (line 27): fractional-second precision p is optional, defaults to no explicit bound, and is allowed from 0 to 6. Inference: an unbounded default still cannot exceed 6 stored digits, so 'unbounded' means 'not declared', not 'arbitrary precision'.

Source claim (lines 47, 231-235): the standard's time-with-time-zone type has 'questionable usefulness' because an offset without a date cannot follow daylight-saving rules, and PostgreSQL explicitly does not recommend it. Inference: any schema retaining timetz is carrying a legacy-compatibility decision that needs an owner, not a neutral type choice.

Source claim (lines 147-159): PostgreSQL never inspects literal content to infer type, so TIMESTAMP '2004-10-19 10:23:54+02' is timestamp without time zone and the offset is silently ignored. Inference: the loss is silent at parse time, so this is a correctness hazard for literals embedded in application code rather than a formatting detail.

Source claim (lines 161-163): timestamptz input is converted to UTC, the stated or assumed zone is not retained, and output is always rendered in the session TimeZone. Inference: the stored value is an instant only; preserving 'the zone the user meant' requires a separate column, which the section does not discuss.

Source claim (lines 169, 188): infinity and -infinity are represented specially and displayed unchanged, while now/today/tomorrow/yesterday are converted at read time and can become stale in prepared statements, views and function definitions. Inference: infinity values participate in ordering and range predicates, so retention and 'expired' queries must decide explicitly how they treat them.

Source claim (line 227): IANA (Olson) data supplies historical rules and future times assume the latest known rules continue indefinitely. Inference: correctness for past and future DST depends on the tzdata shipped with the installation, making it an operational update dependency rather than a static schema property.

Source claim (lines 243-249): abbreviations denote a fixed offset, full names can imply DST rules, and some abbreviations have meant different offsets in different years (MSK example), interpreted as of the specified date. Inference: abbreviations are unsafe as durable stored values or cross-system contract terms; full names plus an explicit zone column are the defensible option.

Source claim (line 299): interval is stored as three integral fields (months, days, microseconds) kept separate because month length varies and a DST day can have 23 or 25 hours. Inference: interval is a calendar-field aggregate, not elapsed physical time, so billing or timeout durations need a stated convention.

Source claim (lines 295-297, 308): unmarked quantities depend on the fields specification, fields to the right of the least significant one are silently discarded, fractional units are converted assuming 30-day months and 24-hour days, and sign handling differs between sql_standard and the traditional interpretation. Inference: interval literals are context- and setting-dependent, which is a portability hazard for stored literals.

Source silence: the section says nothing about clock sources, monotonicity, NTP, or using timestamps as ordering tokens. Inference: nothing here supports treating a stored timestamptz as evidence of event order, which is a question for the book's causal-ordering material rather than this page.

readings.revision: PostgreSQL 17 documentation (docs/17, section 8.1); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed (the Jina wrapper's Published Time 2026-08-13 is a fetch timestamp, not a document revision)
readings.coverage: All 189 lines / 2490 words; sections 8.1 (Table 8.2), 8.1.1 Integer Types, 8.1.2 Arbitrary Precision Numbers, 8.1.3 Floating-Point Types, 8.1.4 Serial Types, including both Notes and the rounding comparison query and its 8-row output; excluded from technical claims: Jina wrapper header lines 1-7 (Title, URL Source, Published Time, Markdown Content), appended heading anchors of the form [#](...), and collapsed table captions such as 'Table 8.2.Numeric Types'; no cookie or navigation chrome was present in the representation

notes: Source claim (Table 8.2, lines 12-23): exact ranges and storage sizes, including numeric's up to 131072 digits before and 16383 after the decimal point, real at 6 digits and double precision at 15 digits of precision. Inference: the digit counts are implementation limits, not design targets, and the table's precision column for floats is decimal digits, not exactness.

Source claim (line 37): numeric calculations are exact where possible (addition, subtraction, multiplication) but 'very slow' compared with integer or floating-point types. Inference: the exactness/throughput trade-off is workload-specific and must be measured, since the section gives no ratio or benchmark.

Source claim (line 37) also recommends numeric 'especially for storing monetary amounts'. Inference: the type removes binary representation error but does not remove rounding-policy choices, so a monetary claim still depends on declared scale and rounding rules the section describes separately.

Source claim (line 57): the maximum precision that can be explicitly declared is 1000, while an unconstrained numeric is governed by Table 8.2's storage limits. Inference: declared precision is a schema-level cap that users often confuse with the much larger physical limit.

Source claim (lines 65-73, 77): since PostgreSQL 15 a numeric column may declare a negative scale (NUMERIC(2,-3) rounds to thousands) or a scale larger than precision (NUMERIC(3,5) holds only fractional values), and such declarations are outside the SQL standard and may not be portable. Inference: these forms encode a business rounding rule inside a type declaration, which is a modeling decision with portability cost.

Source claim (lines 99-115): numeric rounds ties away from zero while real and double precision round ties to the nearest even number, illustrated by -3.5 to 3.5. Inference: the same aggregate or reconciliation computed in numeric versus float8 can disagree exactly at .5 boundaries, so cross-type comparisons need an explicit conversion policy.

Source claim (lines 119-127): real and double precision are IEEE 754 implementations, inexact, and 'comparing two floating-point values for equality might not always work as expected'. Inference: floating-point columns used as keys, join predicates or idempotency tokens are a contract hazard, not merely a precision concern.

Source claim (lines 131-143): output defaults to shortest-precise decimal (at most 17 significant digits for float8, 9 for float4), and extra_float_digits can restore rounded output (0 gives 6 or 15 digits; negative values reduce further). Inference: text renderings of floats depend on server version and session parameter, so exported text is not a stable interchange representation.

Source claim (lines 95, 155): PostgreSQL treats NaN as equal to itself and greater than all non-NaN values, for both numeric and floating-point types, to allow sorting and tree-based indexes. Inference: this deliberately contradicts IEEE comparison semantics and therefore affects range predicates, ORDER BY, and any 'greater than' retention or threshold logic.

Source claim (lines 165-179): smallserial, serial and bigserial are not true types but notational conveniences expanding to a sequence, an integer column with NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval(...), and ALTER SEQUENCE ... OWNED BY. Inference: sequences are separate schema objects, so grants, backups, and migration tooling must handle them explicitly rather than assuming a single column.

Source claim (line 183): gaps can appear even without deletes because a value allocated from the sequence is used up when the inserting transaction rolls back. Inference: serial values must not be read as counts, ordering guarantees, or gapless identifiers in an external contract.

Source claim (line 187): serial/serial4 create integer columns, bigserial/serial8 create bigint, smallserial/serial2 create smallint. Inference: the choice is a range decision made at design time, and the section is silent on the table-rewrite and downtime cost of changing it later.

notes: Source: the page frames collation as per-column or per-operation override of database-level LC_COLLATE and LC_CTYPE, which cannot be changed after database creation (line 8).

Source: derivation is three-tier: any explicit COLLATE must agree and wins; otherwise matching implicit collation or the default; conflicting non-default implicit collations yield an indeterminate collation that errors only where the operation needs it (lines 20-26).
Source: an operator that ignores collation, such as ||, still propagates the combined input collation, so ORDER BY a || b fails while ORDER BY a || 'foo' sorts under de_DE (lines 62-72).
Source: distinct collation objects are incompatible even when behavior is identical; comparing C with POSIX raises an error, and mixing stripped and non-stripped names is discouraged (lines 117-121).
Source: libc collations bind LC_COLLATE and LC_CTYPE plus the database encoding; ICU collations map to one named collator and are encoding-independent (lines 78-80).

Source: ucs_basic and C are described as stable across versions, pg_c_utf8 as stable within a major version, and unicode (UCA with the default element table, equivalent to the ICU root locale) may change with a different ICU build (lines 87-93).
Inference: the page qualifies stability by provider and version, so a persisted ordering or uniqueness contract needs provider and version, not only a locale name.

Source: predefined collations come from operating-system locales discovered by initdb at cluster initialization; locales added later need CREATE COLLATION or pg_import_system_collations (lines 105, 111-113).

Source: nondeterministic collations are opt-in via deterministic = false and may treat different byte sequences as equal; all predefined collations and user-defined collations by default are deterministic (lines 177-188).

Source: listed costs of nondeterministic collations are a performance penalty, no B-tree deduplication, and no pattern matching; normalize and is normalized are offered as an alternative with different trade-offs (lines 188-192).
Inference: an equality-semantics change therefore reaches indexes, uniqueness constraints and pattern predicates, not only ORDER BY.

Source: ICU behavior is set through BCP 47 tags with an -x-icu suffix and keys co, ka, kb, kc, kf, kn, kk, kr, ks, kv; many settings need deterministic = false, and ka-shifted gates several of them (lines 247-270).

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: 19.6. Replication
readings.revision: PostgreSQL 17 (page footer shows 17.11); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed

notes: Source: the section scopes streaming replication (primary and standby, with cascading standbys also sending) and logical replication (publishers and subscribers, one server can be both) (lines 40-44).

Source: sending-server parameters keep their role and meaning after a standby becomes primary, and the primary is always a sending server (line 48). Inference: these settings must be provisioned on every promotion candidate, not only the current primary.

Source: max_wal_senders defaults to 10, 0 disables replication, it is start-only, abrupt disconnects can leave an orphaned slot until timeout, and a standby must set it at least as high as the primary or queries are disallowed (lines 51-53).

Source: max_replication_slots defaults to 10, is start-only, and setting it below existing slots prevents startup; the same parameter name also applies on subscribers with a different meaning (lines 56-58, 217-220). Inference: one identifier carries two separate capacity budgets.

Source: wal_keep_size is a minimum retention with default 0 (no extra segments); the sender may still remove a needed segment and terminate the connection, and archive recovery can rescue the standby (lines 82-84).

Source: max_slot_wal_keep_size defaults to -1 (unlimited); if a slot restart_lsn falls too far behind, required WAL may be removed and the standby may be unable to continue (line 87). Inference: unlimited retention is a storage commitment, not a safety guarantee.
Source: wal_sender_timeout defaults to 60 seconds, 0 disables it, and different values per geographic location are explicitly suggested for low- and high-latency standbys (lines 90-92).

Source: synchronous_standby_names accepts FIRST n (priority) and ANY n (quorum over the listed standbys), the legacy bare list equals FIRST 1, * matches any name, and duplicate names have indeterminate priority (lines 106-124). Inference: this is a commit-wait set over named standbys, not a voter majority.

Source: synchronized_standby_slots makes logical WAL senders wait for named physical slots, logical replication stops if those slots are missing or invalidated, and those standbys need sync_replication_slots = true (lines 134-137, 208-211).

Source: max_standby_archive_delay and max_standby_streaming_delay default to 30 seconds with -1 meaning wait forever; the page stresses each is a per-segment or post-receipt budget, not a maximum query runtime (lines 158-166).

Source: recovery_min_apply_delay delays only commit records, is honored except in crash recovery, accumulates WAL, delays hot_standby_feedback, and with synchronous_commit = remote_apply makes every COMMIT wait (lines 189-204). Inference: a freshness buffer also becomes a commit-latency and storage knob.

Source: subscriber defaults are 4 logical workers (start-only, drawn from max_worker_processes), 2 sync workers per subscription (one per table), and 2 parallel apply workers per subscription (lines 222-243). Inference: the 4-worker default interacts with max_worker_processes, whose sizing this page does not state.

sections: 13.2 Transaction Isolation: SQL-standard levels, prohibited phenomena, Table 13.1, SET TRANSACTION, sequence caveat
notes: Source claim (lines 8-12, 13.1): MVCC gives each SQL statement a snapshot (a 'database version'), prevents statements from seeing inconsistent data written by concurrent transactions, and minimizes lock contention because read locks never conflict with write locks; the no-blocking guarantee is said to hold even at Serializable via SSI.

Source claim (lines 20-36): the SQL standard defines Serializable semantically (same effect as some one-at-a-time order) and the other three levels by prohibited phenomena - dirty read, nonrepeatable read, phantom read, serialization anomaly - and the standard's definition of Serializable is said to rule out all four.

Source claim (lines 40-49, Table 13.1): PostgreSQL accepts all four level names but implements three behaviors - Read Uncommitted is mapped to Read Committed - and its Repeatable Read forbids phantom reads, a stronger guarantee the standard permits because it states only minimum prohibitions.

Source claim (lines 51-55): an explicit Important note carves sequences (and serial counters) out of transaction isolation: their changes are immediately visible to other transactions and are not rolled back on abort.

Source claim (lines 59-61): Read Committed takes a fresh snapshot per command; SELECT sees only data committed before the query began, while UPDATE/DELETE/SELECT FOR UPDATE/SHARE may encounter a concurrently updated row, wait for the other transaction, and then re-evaluate the WHERE clause against the updated version.

Source claim (lines 63-67): ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE can update a row no version of which is conventionally visible to the command; ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING can skip an insert for the same reason; MERGE re-evaluates its actions from the first action against the updated row and raises a uniqueness error rather than restarting MATCHED evaluation.

Source claim (lines 69-87): a Read Committed updating command can see an inconsistent snapshot (concurrent effects on the rows it touches but not on other rows), which the page calls unsuitable for complex search conditions; its two example DELETE statements show when this matters.

Source claim (lines 93-99): Repeatable Read fixes the snapshot at the first non-transaction-control statement of the transaction, not per statement; it prevents all Table 13.1 phenomena except serialization anomalies, and applications must be prepared to retry.

Source claim (lines 99-109): a Repeatable Read transaction that tries to modify or lock a row changed after its snapshot is rolled back with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'; only updating transactions might need retry, because read-only transactions at this level never have serialization conflicts; a read-only control-record/detail-record example shows the view is stable but not serial.

Source claim (lines 111-115): Repeatable Read is identified as academic Snapshot Isolation, distinguished from serializability and from other products' naming, and the page records that before 9.1 Serializable requests produced exactly today's Repeatable Read behavior.

Source claim (lines 119-152): Serializable is SSI - Repeatable Read plus monitoring for read/write dependencies, using non-blocking predicate locks visible in pg_locks as SIReadLock; the mytab SUM example produces SQLSTATE 40001 'could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions'; read data must not be trusted until commit except in DEFERRABLE read-only transactions; SIRead locks may be coarsened and are often kept past commit; even SSI can surface unique-constraint violations absent from true serial execution.

Inference: this is a mechanism-and-guarantee reference, not an evaluation; it reports no overhead measurements, failure rates, or benchmarks for SSI versus locking, and the tuning bullets (max_pred_locks_per_*, random_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost) are advisory and workload-dependent. Representation note: lines 134 and 138 render 'class``= 2' with a doubled backtick, an extraction artifact that does not change meaning.
