readings.coverage: All 79 lines / 1,150 words; Patching definition, the four replay/non-replay behavior cases, the two-unexpected-behaviors summary, deployment implications and the if/elif recommendation read; Jina header fields, zero-width-space heading anchors and 'Direct link to' titles excluded as chrome; code samples flattened but present.
readings.omissions: Linked SDK/patching docs and code samples not read; no execution; no live-page comparison.
readings.representation_gap: No content section appears absent; the only loss is formatting - the two code samples at lines 75 and 79 are flattened into single-line inline code, so newlines and indentation are gone though branches and comments remain legible.
sections: Detailed description of the patched() function
Behavior when replaying with marker before-or-at current location
Behavior when replaying with marker after current location
Behavior when replaying with no marker for that patch ID
A summary of the two potentially unexpected behaviors
notes: Source claim (line 10): a Patch is a logical branch in a Workflow for one change, compared to a feature flag; its purpose is to apply code to new Workflow Executions without disrupting in-progress ones.
Source claim (line 14): the detailed semantics that follow are scoped to the patched() function in the Python, .NET, and Ruby SDKs; the page does not describe equivalent primitives in other SDKs.

Source claim (lines 18-21): when not replaying, the first encounter adds a marker to the event history, upserts a search attribute and returns true; later blocks see the marker, leave history unchanged and return true.

Source claim (lines 27-33): when replaying with a marker at the same location, the execution writes a marker to the replay event history and returns true; if the marker is earlier in the history, it returns true without modifying the replay history.

Source claim (line 37): a marker after the current execution point means the new patch is too early; the execution attempts to write the marker and throws a non-deterministic exception because replay and original histories differ.

Source claim (lines 41-45): when replaying with no marker for that ID, patched() returns false and adds nothing - and all later calls with that ID also return false, even after replay ends, contradicting the non-replay 'always true' rule; the page flags this as the caveat to its earlier description.

Source claim (lines 51-56): the summary states two unexpected behaviors - history after the current location matters (a later marker gives non-determinism, an absent marker gives false), and a miss during replay latches false for the remainder of that execution.

Source claim (lines 60-67): after a deploy, in-flight executions replay to their shutdown point and do not follow patched branches; afterwards they use new code only if no patched() call with that ID occurred during replay, otherwise they run non-patched code. The stated rationale is that later patched code depending on earlier patched code must keep the old path, while independent new code may switch.

Source claim (line 69): the documented consequence is explicit - a Workflow does not always run the newest code; it does so only when not replaying, or when replay is surpassed and the ID never appeared in the replay.

Source claim (lines 73-77): the recommendation is to put the newest version first in an if/elif chain of patched('v3'), patched('v2') and else, because when not replaying patched() returns true; the counterexample shows v2-first making new executions take v2 and never reach v3.

Inference: the page explains one SDK family's runtime behavior; it states no cross-SDK equivalence, no policy for eventually removing old patches or markers, no limits on patch-ID proliferation, and no production failure data. The 'marker plus search attribute' mechanism is described operationally, not as a schema or query contract.
Representation note: heading anchors include a zero-width space and 'Direct link to ...' titles; code samples are flattened as described in representation_gap. No claim here rests on indentation.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Does the durable-workflow page treat code versioning of in-flight executions as a first-class compatibility problem, distinct from compensating-action design?
Does the failure page include non-determinism from history/code mismatch as a failure class distinct from timeouts, task failures and retry exhaustion?
Should progressive delivery cover long-lived workflow code as a compatibility surface with its own deploy-time branching rule (newest branch first)?
Does canary compatibility account for executions that span a deploy and replay old history, where rolling back code may not restore prior behavior?
Does the messaging-versus-durable-workflow comparison note that replay determinism constrains how new code may be introduced into running executions?

readings.unit: Complete page: etcd API guarantees
readings.revision: Live public docs, version-pinned to /docs/v3.6; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed. Page footer records 'Last modified September 26, 2025' (commit 5e64060, PR #984) as the closest available revision marker.
readings.coverage: All 1023 lines / 4286 words read end to end. The page is mostly chrome: technical body is lines 915-996 (11 sections, ~1066 prose words once link targets are stripped, about 25% of the tokenised text); lines 1-350 are the site header plus version selector, 350-895 are the multi-version left navigation linked for nine doc versions (830 etcd.io links; 100+ each for v3.8, v3.7, v3.6), and lines 997-1023 are the feedback widget, last-modified note, social links and footer. Excluded from technical claims: the entire navigation tree, breadcrumb trailer (lines 910-913), 'Edit this page'/'Create child page' tools, 'On this page' anchor list (lines 896-908), and the feedback/footer block. Sections covered: APIs to consider; KV APIs; Durability; Strict serializability; Atomicity; Linearizability; Watch APIs; Lease APIs; etcd specific definitions; Operation completed; Revision.
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read: etcd API reference and concurrency API reference (Range/Put/Delete/Txn/Watch/Grant/KeepAlive), the 'why' page section 'notes on the usage of lock and lease', design-client and design-auth-v3, Jepsen consistency-model page, the Herlihy-Wing linearizability paper, and the Stanford leases paper. No cluster, lease, watch or compaction behaviour was executed. Representation artefact: 'Revoke' in the API list (line 934) is plain text with no target, unlike its six siblings.
notes: Source claim (line 919): etcd 'ensures the strongest consistency and durability guarantees for a distributed system'. Inference: this is the maintainers' specification of intent, offered without proof or measurement; it ranks the API contract, not a deployment.

Source claim (lines 945, 949): durability attaches to completed operations, all accessible data is durable, and a read never returns data that was not made durable. Inference: the guarantee is scoped to what the server committed through consensus, and the page separately concedes (line 992) that a client can be unsure whether its own operation completed.

Source claim (line 953): KV operations are atomic and occur in a total order consistent with real-time order, with the total order implied by revision. Inference: strict serializability is asserted per API surface, so combining etcd reads with an external store needs a separate argument the page does not make.

Source claim (line 955): operation order inside a transaction matches the listed order only when there are no nested TXNs; for nested TXNs the order of execution 'is not specified'. Inference: nested TXN is the single place where the page withdraws a guarantee, making transaction shape a correctness variable rather than style.

Source claim (line 961): atomicity extends to watch, because all events produced by one operation arrive in one watch response and partial events are never observed. Inference: watch atomicity is bounded by one operation, not by a multi-operation transaction.

Source claim (line 969): linearizability is the default for all other operations, while a client-selected 'serializable' mode may return quorum-stale data and skips live consensus. Inference: the stale-read mode is an explicitly supported downgrade, so a read path must record which mode produced a value.

Source claim (lines 975-980): watch guarantees are ordered by revision, unique, reliable within the available history window, atomic per revision, resumable from the last received revision, and bookmarkable. Inference: reliability and resumability are both conditioned on the history window that compaction truncates, so watch dependability is a retention property, not an absolute one.

Source claim (line 982): etcd 'does not ensure linearizability for watch operations' and users must verify event revisions. Inference: this refutes the common shorthand that etcd is linearizable period, and it is the sentence a lease/fence argument should rest on.

Source claim (line 941): in a correctly working cluster watch events are expected about 10 ms after the event, yet 'there is no limit' and events in unhealthy clusters 'might never arrive'. Inference: 10 ms is an expectation, not a bound or SLO; no timeout or latency budget should be derived from it.

Source claim (line 986): a lease is granted, attached by put, revoked, and expired by wall-clock TTL, with distributed locks as the primary use case; correct lock usage is deferred to a separate 'why' page. Inference: this page alone does not license a lock protocol, so the deferred page is a real evidence dependency rather than optional reading.

Source claim (line 992): an operation is complete once committed through consensus; a client may be uncertain after a timeout or network disruption, and etcd may abort operations during a leader election without sending abort responses to outstanding requests. Inference: ambiguous client outcomes are documented behaviour, so retry safety must come from operation identity, not from error signalling.

Source claim (line 996): each modifying operation gets one increasing revision, a transaction gets one revision however many keys it touched, and equal revisions mean 'concurrently' modified. Inference: revision is a transaction-ordering clock, not a per-key version counter, so it cannot stand in for an ETag-style single-key token. Scope note: all eleven sections come from 82 body lines, so this record covers a short normative page, not an implementation guide.

tycho_candidates.candidate: The page already cites this URL for 'KV ordering, leases and delayed watches'; add that watch notifications are explicitly non-linearizable, so a watch event is not a write fence, and record src.etcd-api-enrichment in the chapter source ledger.
Sharpen the agreement-versus-linearizability section with etcd's own split: linearizable KV by default, an opted-in stale read mode, and no linearizability guarantee for watch.

Contrast a local relational isolation level with etcd's strict-serializability claim and its nested-TXN ordering gap, as a case where the store specifies ordering only for a restricted transaction shape.

Use the 'operation completed' definition — timeout or partition leaves the client uncertain, and leader election can abort requests without an abort response — as a documented example of an ambiguous effect needing operation identity.
Ask whether an etcd revision carried as a log-position token can supply monotonic reads across client reconnects, given that watches are resumable only inside the compaction window.

readings.unit: Complete page: How to prevent object overwrites with conditional writes
readings.revision: Live public docs (Amazon S3 User Guide, 'latest' alias); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed. The representation carries no last-modified date, no document version and no revision identifier.
readings.coverage: All 1765 lines / 7469 words read end to end. The page is mostly chrome: the technical body is lines 1439-1668 (six sections, ~2221 prose words once link targets are stripped, about 34% of the tokenised text). Lines 6-74 are the cookie-preferences and privacy-choices panels, 76-1438 are the AWS docs shell plus the whole Amazon S3 User Guide left navigation (831 S3 userguide links across buckets, objects, vectors, security and reference topics), and 1669-1765 are the feedback widget, related resources, next/previous topic links, site footer and two duplicated image lightbox modals. Excluded from technical claims: cookie and privacy panels, the entire navigation tree, breadcrumbs (lines 1428-1437), PDF/RSS/Markdown download links, the 'Agent Setup' promo, 'Focus mode' control, the help-us feedback prompts, and the lightbox repeats at lines 1755-1765. Sections covered: How to prevent object overwrites based on key names; Conditional Put/Copy/multipart upload Using the AWS CLI (If-None-Match); How to prevent overwrites if the object has changed; Conditional Put/Copy/multipart upload Using the AWS CLI (If-Match); Conditional write behavior; Conditional write scenarios (conditional writes during multipart uploads, concurrent deletes during multipart uploads).
readings.omissions: Linked pages not read: PutObject, CopyObject and CompleteMultipartUpload API references; 'Enforce conditional writes on Amazon S3 buckets'; 'How to retrieve or copy objects based on metadata'; object-key naming; ETag/Content-MD5 integrity page; AWS CLI put-object/copy-object/complete-multipart-upload references; lifecycle AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload configuration. Two embedded scenario diagrams (conwrite_put_mpu.png, conwrite_delete_mpu.png) were not viewed; only their alt text was available. No request was executed against any bucket.
sections: How to prevent object overwrites based on key names
Conditional Put Using the AWS CLI (If-None-Match)
Conditional Copy Using the AWS CLI (If-None-Match)
Conditional multipart upload Using the AWS CLI (If-None-Match)
How to prevent overwrites if the object has changed
Conditional Put Using the AWS CLI (If-Match)
Conditional Copy Using the AWS CLI (If-Match)
Conditional multipart upload Using the AWS CLI (If-Match)
notes: Source claim (lines 1459-1463, 1485): conditional writes attach an HTTP If-None-Match or If-Match header to WRITE requests, and If-None-Match with the '*' value makes the write fail when the key already exists. Inference: this is create-if-absent built on standard HTTP precondition semantics, so it cannot serve as a general compare-and-swap over mutable content.

Source claim (line 1469): conditional writes require AWS Signature Version 4. Inference: the capability is unavailable to any client still signing with a legacy scheme, so adoption is a client-migration dependency and not only a write-path edit.

Source claim (line 1491): If-None-Match 'only applies to the current version of an object in a version bucket'. Inference: a caller cannot express 'no version of this key has ever existed', so historical versions are invisible to this precondition.

Source claim (lines 1493, 1555): If-None-Match needs only s3:PutObject, while If-Match needs s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject. Inference: the two preconditions have different authorization footprints, so a least-privilege policy written for create-if-absent cannot silently support ETag preconditions.

Source claim (line 1553): an object's ETag is 'a string that's unique to the object and reflects a change to the object's content', and If-Match fails when the supplied value does not match. Inference: the strength of If-Match rests entirely on the caller's assumption that this ETag identifies the bytes it validated; the page promises nothing further about ETag derivation.

Source claim (line 1620): when several conditional writes target the same object name, the first write to finish succeeds and later writes get 412 Precondition Failed. Inference: 'first to finish' is a completion-order rule, so request arrival time cannot predict the winner.

Source claim (lines 1618, 1631-1636): if the current version is a delete marker or absent, If-None-Match succeeds while If-Match fails with 404 Not Found. Inference: the two headers disagree about what a missing or deleted object means, so status-code handling must be keyed to the header actually sent.

Source claim (lines 1622, 1629): a delete that completes before the conditional write yields 409 Conflict for If-None-Match but 404 Not Found for If-Match, and after a 409 a PutObject may be retried whereas a CompleteMultipartUpload must be re-initiated via CreateMultipartUpload. Inference: recovery cost differs by API, so a single generic retry wrapper would silently mishandle the multipart case.

Internal tension in the source (lines 1627-1629): the If-Match paragraph first says a 409 Conflict can occur with concurrent requests, then says a 404 Not Found is returned when a concurrent delete wins; the scenario note (line 1660) settles it as 404 for If-Match, while the multipart note (line 1648) reports 412 for both headers when a conditional completion loses. Inference: the page offers no single status-code table, so an implementation that assumes one code per header will misclassify some races.

Source claim (lines 1644-1650): conditional writes do not consider in-progress multipart uploads because those are not yet fully written objects, so a competing conditional PutObject can win and the later conditional CompleteMultipartUpload then fails with 412 for either header. Inference: an in-flight MPU confers no exclusivity, so 'I started the upload first' is not a lock.

Source claim (line 1668): AWS recommends an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule to bound the cost of incomplete uploads. Inference: the failure mode above creates a standing storage obligation, so enabling conditional multipart completion without that rule leaves a cost leak behind every lost race.

Scope and representation: the page covers preconditions only for PutObject, CopyObject and CompleteMultipartUpload (lines 1495-1501, 1557-1563) and makes no claim about read consistency, replication, directory buckets or non-S3 stores; the CLI examples are printed twice (inline under the explanatory heading, then under a 'Conditional ... Using the AWS CLI' heading at lines 1503-1541 and 1565-1611), which is a conversion artefact rather than extra guidance, and the source text contains the typo 'tnis' at lines 1535 and 1597.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Tighten 'prevent replacement, not only duplication' with the exact scope: If-None-Match is create-if-absent against the current version only, first-completed writer wins, and a delete marker counts as absent — so the precondition protects one key at one instant, not a publication protocol.

Add the documented resolution asymmetry — retry PutObject after 409, but re-run CreateMultipartUpload after 409 or 412 — plus the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload obligation that a lost completion race leaves behind.
Trace the delete-marker case: If-None-Match succeeds and If-Match returns 404 when the current version is a delete marker, so versioning and lifecycle policy change what a conditional write means.
Treat the precondition header as an effect-identity mechanism for create-once publication, and ask what identity survives when the caller must rebuild the request after a 412 instead of a retry.

Use conditional-write 412/409/404 as a worked case of conflict-as-correct-result, where the store refuses the second writer instead of merging, and the caller must classify the refusal before retrying.

readings.unit: Complete page: Data deletion on Google Cloud
readings.revision: Live public docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 85 lines / 2063 words. Sections: Data storage and replication; Data deletion pipeline (Stages 1-4); Deletion timeline; closing media-sanitization text. Chrome excluded: Jina title/URL header, 'Markdown Content:' marker and trailing image link; none carried technical claims. No representation gap: every heading is present and the page ends at its sanitization conclusion.
readings.omissions: Linked Terms of Service, Data Processing Addendum, default-encryption, infrastructure-security, NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1 and DoD 5220.22-M documents not read; pipeline diagram not rendered; linked product pages not read; no provider console inspection, independent test or execution.
sections: Data deletion pipeline: Stage 1, deletion request
Stage 3, logical deletion from active systems
notes: Source claim: the page describes Google Cloud's own secured deletion process, last updated May 2024 with a status-quo disclaimer (line 6). Inference: it is vendor self-description, not an independent audit; internal signal and facility claims are not externally corroborated in this representation.

Source claim: deletion is staged as request, soft deletion, logical deletion from active systems, then expiration from backups (lines 26-65). Inference: 'deleted' is ambiguous until the stage and the observable assertion are named.

Source claim: the timeline sets a 24-hour goal for marking, up to 30 days of recovery, about two months for active-system deletion, and backup expiry within six months (lines 69-73). Inference: these clocks overlap rather than simply sum; no per-object completion date is given.

Qualifier conflict: 'maximum period of about six months (180 days)' (line 69) mixes a bound with an approximation, and Stage 2 is a 'goal' (line 71). Inference: the text supports an order-of-magnitude six-month commitment, not a precise 180-day SLA; do not tighten it downstream.

Source claim: project deletion broadcasts a suspension signal keyed to project number and collects ACKs, with Bigtable tables in recovery up to 30 days (line 45). Inference: this is a distributed control protocol whose retry bounds, partial-failure handling and customer-visible evidence are unspecified.

Source claim: active systems use mark-and-sweep garbage collection and major compaction at regular intervals; Cloud Storage additionally uses cryptographic erasure (lines 51-55). Inference: compaction cadence, not the delete API call, sets physical reclamation time.

Unresolved wording: the text excludes Cloud Storage from the overwrite sentence, then says Cloud Storage is 'also' deleted through cryptographic erasure (lines 53-55). Inference: whether Cloud Storage blocks are overwritten as well is not settled by this page; retain the ambiguity.

Source claim: daily, weekly and monthly aggregate backups are retired on a predefined cycle, and data deleted from active systems is no longer copied into backups (lines 59-63). Inference: backup retention creates a deliberate deletion lag, and pre-deletion snapshots remain readable until expiry unless keys are destroyed.

Source claim: cryptographic erasure can make data unrecoverable before backup expiry (line 65), but key-copy inventory and shared-key blast radius are not discussed. Inference: 'erased' there means key-dependent unreadability; it is not evidence that ciphertext is absent.

Source claim: retired media are zero-overwritten with multi-step verification, otherwise crushed/deformed or shredded, citing NIST SP 800-88 Rev 1 and DoD 5220.22-M (lines 83-85). Inference: these are facility-process assertions; neither the standards nor the page supply per-device evidence to a customer.

Scope: 'customer data' is defined by reference to the Google Cloud Terms (line 8), and contractual deletion commitments live in the DPA (line 12), neither of which is in this representation. Inference: the page describes mechanics, not remedies or current universal deadlines.

Coverage limit: the pipeline diagram (line 77) was not rendered and no deletion, restore or media-sanitization exercise was run. Inference: the page can support a staged model and vocabulary, not a verified erasure outcome.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Already cites this page (line 178); enrich its 'Deletion across derived state and restored backups' table with the four stages and the 30-day/two-month/six-month clocks, keeping the 'about' qualifier.
Contrast backup retention needed for restore/RPO with deletion propagation: a retained snapshot is both a recovery asset and a delayed-erasure liability.
Already lists src.gcp-deletion-enrichment (line 43); add cryptographic erasure and version/backup expiry as distinct lifecycle completion states.
Retention limits need a staged completion vocabulary (marked, logically deleted, key-destroyed, media-sanitized) instead of one 'deleted' flag.
Mark-and-sweep and compaction are the vendor's active-storage deletion analogue: visibility (logical deletion) and space reclamation are separate clocks.
RPO-driven backup cycles impose a deletion lag; recovery objectives and erasure commitments must be co-designed and separately evidenced.

readings.unit: Complete page: Temporal Workflow Execution overview | Temporal Documentation
readings.revision: Live public docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 174 lines / 1645 words. Sections: What is a Workflow Execution?; Replays; Commands and awaitables; What is a Command?; Status; Workflow Execution Chain; Memo; State Transition; Workflow cache. Chrome excluded: on-page table of contents (lines 6-16), repeated 'Direct link to' anchor artifacts, SDK how-to link lists and image captions. No representation gap: all nine listed sections appear in the body, with 'Status' shortened from the ToC label.
readings.omissions: Linked determinism constraints, Event History, Command reference, gRPC proto, Continue-As-New, retry policies, workers/tasks and per-SDK replay pages not read; diagrams not rendered; no product version, quota beyond the 40 KB Memo limit, or execution test; no product use.
notes: Source claim: a Workflow Execution is a durable, reliable, scalable function execution created by running a Workflow Definition; durability is defined as 'the absence of an imposed time limit' (lines 20, 36-38). Inference: this is a product-scoped definition, not a general distributed-systems definition.

Source claim: workflow code executes 'effectively once and to completion' (line 38), not exactly once. Inference: external side effects still need effect identity and idempotency; the page does not claim exactly-once effects.

Source claim: replay resumes progress by checking generated Commands against an existing Event History (line 54), while deterministic constraints are delegated to another page (line 56). Inference: replay correctness depends on deterministic workflow code, which this representation does not examine.

Source claim: an execution issues Commands and waits on Awaitables; a Worker batches Commands when the function can no longer progress without an Awaitable result (lines 68-79). Inference: the Command boundary is where workflow decisions become durable history entries.

Source claim: a Command is a requested action from Worker to Temporal Service after a Workflow Task Execution and is recorded as an Event; WorkflowTaskStarted and WorkflowTaskCompleted always bracket a completion request (lines 92-96). Inference: Event History is the audit substrate, but its retention and size limits are not stated here.

Source claim: status is Open (Running or Paused) or Closed (Cancelled, Completed, Continued-As-New, Failed, Terminated, Timed Out) (lines 106-128). Inference: Paused still counts as Open, so liveness checks must not equate Open with active progress.

Source claim: identity is Namespace plus Workflow Id plus Run Id, while a Chain shares a Workflow Id and links runs through Continue-As-New, Retries or Cron (lines 132-138). Inference: 'same workflow' is ambiguous unless run or chain scope is stated.

Source claim: Workflow Execution Timeout applies to the Chain and Workflow Run Timeout to a single run (line 140). Inference: timeout policy must be scoped to the same identity unit as retention and reporting.

Source claim: Memos are non-indexed, lack type safety, are eventually consistent, should not hold execution-critical data, and are limited to 40 KB on Temporal Cloud (lines 144-156). Inference: Memos are annotation, not workflow state.

Source claim: a simple workflow with two sequential Activities produces 11 State Transitions (two for start, four per Activity, one for completion), each recorded in a persistence store (lines 160-166). The arithmetic is internally consistent; inference: transition count is a cost and throughput driver the page does not quantify.

Source claim: Workers keep an in-memory LRU Workflow Cache, sticky queues route later tasks to the same Worker, and eviction forces Event History replay (lines 168-174). Inference: the cache is subordinate to history, so eviction affects latency rather than correctness.

Scope: the page is a conceptual overview that links determinism, Event History, Command reference, gRPC proto and SDK pages, none included here. Inference: it establishes vocabulary and mechanism shape, not version-specific behavior, limits or exactly-once delivery.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Already cites this URL (line 142); add Command/Awaitable batching, Open/Closed status and chain-versus-run identity, preserving the page's 'does not prove exactly once' caveat.
Separate workflow-state recovery through history replay from business compensation: a durable engine resumes the process but does not make external effects atomic.
Place Event History replay beside outbox and inbox as three durable-coordination mechanisms with different guarantees and different failure boundaries.
'Effectively once' is the source's own wording; use it to argue for effect identity at the Activity boundary rather than exactly-once delivery.
Workflow lifetime outlives Worker, task and cache lifetimes; worker loss is recoverable by replay, not by transferring in-memory state.
A Worker's LRU workflow cache is a latency optimization subordinate to Event History; eviction triggers replay rather than state loss.

readings.unit: Complete page: Key Management - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
readings.revision: Live public docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Linked NIST, ASVS, RFC and companion cheat-sheet targets were not fetched.
readings.reader: Delegated reader batch 9; parent validation pending.
readings.coverage: All 299 lines / 4449 words; sections Introduction through References (27 headings incl. all subsections); chrome excluded (lines 1-7 reader title/URL/published-time header and permalink glyphs).
notes: Source claim: this is implementation guidance for application key management, not a standard or certification; it cites NIST SP 800-57/800-133/800-38D, FIPS 140-2/140-3, FIPS 180/186/198 and OWASP ASVS 5.0. Inference: no compliance conclusion follows from this page alone.

Source claim: key selection starts from application security objectives (confidentiality at rest and in transit, device and data-origin authenticity, integrity, key-encryption keys), not from library availability. Inference: this supports a requirements-first gate before algorithm selection.

Source claim: a single key should serve one purpose; the stated reasons are cross-use weakening, blast-radius limitation and conflicting retention periods. Inference: purpose separation needs KMS key-usage policy or equivalent enforcement, which the page does not specify.

Source claim: representative cryptoperiods include symmetric data-encryption originator use up to 2 years (general low volume) or a day/week (high volume or link encryption), recipient decryption up to 3 years beyond originator use, signing keys 1-3 years, and static key-establishment pairs 1-2 years. Inference: these are risk-assessed examples, not universal defaults.

Source claim: with AES-GCM and random 96-bit IVs, each key is limited to at most 2^32 encryption operations across all devices sharing that key (NIST SP 800-38D Section 8.3). Inference: the cap is per key, so key sharding changes accounting but not the per-key limit.

Source claim: retiring a KEK requires rewrapping stored DEKs; rewrap leaves DEKs and their cryptoperiod/usage counters unchanged, while replacing a DEK for existing ciphertext requires re-encryption; managed services may retain old wrapping-key versions. Inference: rotation is several distinct operations and provider behavior must be verified per service.

Source claim: keys and secrets must never be committed to repositories or embedded in build artifacts; use a secrets manager/key vault, keep raw keys out of application code, and perform cryptographic operations inside the module boundary, with HSM/TPM preferred at higher assurance. Inference: this is a control objective, not evidence of vault authorization or audit quality.

Source claim: a compromise-recovery plan must name notification and recovery personnel, the re-key method, a key inventory, revocation-checking policy and re-key monitoring. Inference: plan existence is organizational evidence that document review cannot verify.

Source claim: destruction is the final lifecycle state; destroy all copies including backup, archive, escrow and memory copies; cryptographic erasure is acceptable only when all protecting keys and plaintext copies are gone; software overwrite is best-effort in managed runtimes. Inference: 'destroyed' is therefore probabilistic in garbage-collected runtimes and stronger with HSM zeroize.

Source claim: trust stores need controls against third-party root injection, integrity protection, authenticated key export and a secure update process. Inference: trust-store update is a supply-chain trust boundary comparable to artifact signing.

Source claim: 'Never escrow keys used for performing digital signatures' while encryption keys may be escrowed. Inference: the prohibition is stated absolutely; any exception needs separate authority and is not supported by this page.

Representation/quality: line 116 ends with an unmatched ')' after the NIST SP 800-57 reference and line 251 embeds 'i.' inside numbered item 8. These look like formatting defects, not technical assertions; no technical text appears absent.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Extend the cryptographic isolation row with key purpose separation, cryptoperiods, rewrap-versus-reencrypt and the HSM/module boundary as explicit conditions.
Add key-rotation/revocation, zeroization limits in managed runtimes and trust-store injection to the credential failure-mode list.
Sharpen the distinction between artifact signing keys and release credentials with rotation, revocation and trust-root scope.
Qualify signature validity: a verified signature does not establish key-holder authority or authorization for a target environment.
Add key custody, HSM, automated rotation and compromise-recovery drills as lifecycle operating-cost line items.

readings.unit: Complete page: REST Security - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
readings.revision: Live public docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Linked NIST, ASVS, RFC and companion cheat-sheet targets were not fetched.
readings.reader: Delegated reader batch 9; parent validation pending.
readings.coverage: All 268 lines / 3359 words; sections Introduction through References (22 headings incl. subsections); chrome excluded (lines 1-7 reader title/URL/published-time header and permalink glyphs); response-header tables sit under the Audit logs heading with no separate heading (text present; heading flattening only).
notes: Source claim: REST follows Fielding's dissertation, with resources identified by URIs, representations, client/server plus cache/resolver/tunnel connectors, statelessness and HATEOAS. Inference: these are definitional commitments, not security controls.

Source claim: 'stateless' refers to resource state, not session state, and stateful APIs plus client-to-backend state passing are out of scope or anti-patterns. Inference: the later JWT denylist recommendation adds server-side state, a tension the page does not reconcile.

Source claim: secure REST services must expose only HTTPS endpoints; mutually authenticated client certificates are suggested for highly privileged services. Inference: transport protection does not cover token storage, logging or endpoint compromise.

Source claim: access control should be decided locally at each endpoint while authentication is centralized in an IdP that issues access tokens. Inference: central issuance does not centralize object-level authorization.

Source claim: reject 'alg':'none'; prefer signatures over MACs because every MAC-validating service can mint tokens; verify integrity from local configuration, not the token header; require and validate iss/aud/exp per RFC 9068 and nbf where the profile requires it; denylist jti on explicit session termination. Inference: MAC trust-domain coupling is the key architectural point.

Source claim: API keys are required on every request to a protected endpoint, 429 is returned for excessive rate, keys are revoked on agreement violation, and API keys alone must not protect sensitive resources. Inference: API keys identify clients, not users or objects.

Source claim: allowlist HTTP methods, return 405 for non-matching requests, and authorize the method on collection, action and record; Java EE verb tampering is cited as a common misconfiguration. Inference: 405 discloses route existence, a trade-off against 404 that the page does not discuss.

Source claim: workflows such as create-validate-approve-finalize need server-side state-transition validation, explicit state machines, stage-bound tokens and rejection of out-of-order transitions, plus a four-question test checklist. Inference: per-endpoint authentication cannot detect sequence abuse, so workflow state becomes an authorization input.

Source claim: validate length/range/format/type, use strong types and regexes, reject unexpected content, cap request size with 413, log validation failures and use XXE-safe parsers. Inference: logging validation failures can itself create a sensitive-data channel if raw inputs are recorded.

Source claim: require a supported Content-Type on bodied requests and return 415, reserve 406 for response negotiation, never copy Accept into Content-Type, and declare consumes/produces explicitly. Inference: 406/415 confusion is a contract defect that changes client retry behavior.

Source claim: browser-facing responses should carry Cache-Control no-store (which the Cache API ignores), CSP frame-ancestors 'none', Content-Type, HSTS (initial HTTP remains exposed and trusted attacker certificates are not covered), nosniff and legacy X-Frame-Options; other headers matter only for HTML. Inference: 'all API responses' is broader than the stated browser rationale.

Source claim: return generic errors without stack traces; write audit logs before and after security events, log token-validation errors and sanitize log data against injection; use semantically appropriate status codes. Inference: durability, integrity and retention are unspecified, so this sheet alone cannot support an audit-evidence claim.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add a status-code and content-negotiation table (405/406/413/415/429) as transport-contract evidence, kept distinct from domain effect.
Use the out-of-order workflow example as a negative test: sequence authorization is not supplied by per-endpoint authentication.
Clarify that Content-Type and consumes/produces are compatibility contracts, not merely schema-version metadata.
Cross-link JWT iss/aud/exp validation and API-key limitations to per-object and per-tenant authorization.
Add log-injection sanitization and pre/post security-event logging as evidence-quality constraints on audit records.

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: Google SRE- DNS Load Balancing For Traffic Distribution
readings.revision: Public SRE book chapter (sre.google web edition); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 87 lines / 2650 words; three H2 sections (Load Balancing at the Frontend; Power Isn't the Answer, which carries the DNS discussion; Load Balancing at the Virtual IP Address); chrome excluded (lines 1-7 Jina title, URL, published-time and 'Markdown Content' header). The reader title 'Google SRE- DNS Load Balancing For Traffic Distribution' is auto-generated and differs from the chapter's own H1 'Load Balancing at the Frontend'; it was not used as a technical claim.
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Bibliography entries (Con15, Kar97, Eis16, Han94, Moc87) and footnote targets 103-105 not fetched; DNS RFCs consulted only through the chapter's own statements. No sidebar, cookie banner or navigation text was present in the representation.
sections: Load Balancing at the Virtual IP Address
notes: Source claim: even a hypothetical single supercomputer is rejected because it remains a single point of failure and is bounded by the speed of light over fiber. Inference: the argument disqualifies vertical consolidation on reliability and physics grounds, not merely on cost or throughput.

Source claim: optimal global distribution depends on the request; a search is sent to the nearest datacenter by RTT, while a video upload may take an underutilized link to maximize throughput at some latency cost. Inference: 'optimal' is workload-defined, so one global policy cannot be correct for both request types.

Source claim: inside a datacenter, machines are treated as equally distant on one network, so local balancing targets utilization and protecting a single server. Inference: global and local selection optimize different objectives and can legitimately disagree.

Source claim: the simplest DNS approach returns several A/AAAA records and lets clients pick arbitrarily; SRV weights and priorities are not adopted for HTTP. Inference: the fallback policy executes in client software the operator does not control or observe.

Source claim: anycast authoritative nameservers plus a maintained network-to-location map can approximate proximity, but require a complex DNS implementation and a pipeline that keeps the map current. Inference: proximity steering is itself a stateful service with its own staleness failure mode.

Source claim: recursive resolvers hide the client address, so replies can only be tuned for resolver-to-nameserver distance unless EDNS0 client subnet is used, which is not yet standard though large resolvers support it. Inference: resolver topology becomes part of the load-balancing correctness argument, not just a networking detail.

Source claim: one authoritative reply can reach one user or thousands because resolvers cache within the TTL; Google therefore tracks resolver population size and geography. Inference: a DNS decision is also a blast-radius decision, and TTL is a lower bound on convergence, not an acknowledgment that clients switched.

Source claim: DNS replies must fit the 512-byte RFC 1035 limit, bounding addresses per reply well below fleet size, so VIP-level balancing must follow. Inference: the two-layer design is structural rather than an optimization.

Source claim: VIPs are shared addresses; 'id(packet) mod N' avoids per-connection state, but removing one backend changes N and remaps almost every connection, resetting stateful sessions. Inference: statelessness buys failure coupling, and consistent hashing is presented as a degraded-mode fallback rather than the default.

Source claim: consistent hashing (1997) keeps the mapping relatively stable when backends are added or removed, and is used when the system is under pressure such as a DoS attack. Inference: the chapter treats connection tracking as normal operation and hashing as the pressure valve.

Source claim: NAT needs a per-connection table; layer-2 MAC rewriting enables Direct Server Response so replies bypass the balancer, but requires one broadcast domain, which Google outgrew. Inference: DSR savings scale with the request/reply size asymmetry, and its limit is topological rather than algorithmic.

Source claim: the current design encapsulates with GRE and the backend strips the outer header, removing the shared-broadcast-domain requirement at 24 bytes IPv4+GRE overhead that can exceed MTU and force fragmentation, mitigated by a larger intra-datacenter MTU. Inference: topology independence is paid per packet and depends on a path-MTU contract the chapter leaves implicit.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add resolver caching, EDNS0 client-subnet and anycast-proximity limits as constraints on DNS-derived routing; keep DNS convergence distinct from endpoint readiness.
Use VIP forwarding (DSR/GRE) and consistent hashing as reasons connection identity outlives a backend-list change, and tie hash stability to the drain window.
Cite mod-N remapping failure and consistent hashing as placement-stability evidence, while noting the source frames hashing as a load-balancer fallback, not a shard-assignment proof.
Distinguish minimal-remap hashing from bounded-overlap shuffle sharding; hashed assignment alone does not establish independence.
Record cache warmth as a legitimate reason to route past the nearest datacenter, so proximity is one routing objective among several.

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: Boost Efficacy with Network Load Balancer
readings.revision: Public SRE book chapter (sre.google web edition); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 224 lines / 5604 words; five H2 sections (Load Balancing in the Datacenter; The Ideal Case; Identifying Bad Tasks: Flow Control and Lame Ducks; Limiting the Connections Pool with Subsetting; Load Balancing Policies); chrome excluded (lines 1-5 Jina title, URL and 'Markdown Content' header). The reader title 'Boost Efficacy with Network Load Balancer' is auto-generated and differs from the chapter's own H1 'Load Balancing in the Datacenter'; it was not used as a technical claim.
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Six figure images (Figure 20-1 to 20-6) were not rendered or inspected; their values are reported only as the prose states them, and captions/alt text were read as text. The linked overload-handling chapter and bibliography were not fetched.
sections: Identifying Bad Tasks: Flow Control and Lame Ducks
Limiting the Connections Pool with Subsetting
notes: Source claim: the model assumes homogeneous interchangeable backend processes, at least three and sometimes more than 10,000, typically 100-1,000, with clients selecting a backend per query. Inference: the policies are analyzed under a symmetry that the later machine-diversity discussion concedes real fleets do not have.

Source claim: with uneven load, usable capacity is capped by the most loaded task and waste is the sum over tasks of CPU[0] minus CPU[i], so 1,000 reserved CPUs may yield only about 700 usable. Inference: reserved capacity overstates usable capacity, and part of the gap is a deliberate latency margin rather than pure inefficiency.

Source claim: a client-side active-request limit near 100 is crude flow control that can backfire, leaving requests blocked until timeout, especially with long-lived requests. Inference: a fixed per-connection concurrency cap can turn slow backends into a total outage of the pool.

Source claim: backends are healthy, refusing connections or lame duck; lame duck is broadcast to active clients and reaches inactive clients through periodic UDP health checks within 1-2 RTT. Inference: drain propagation needs a second channel precisely because idle clients hold no connection to update.

Source claim: shutdown is SIGTERM, then lame duck, then in-flight requests complete, then exit or kill after a configured interval of 10-150 s depending on client complexity. Inference: that interval is a budget derived from the request-duration distribution; too short produces errors and too long slows every maintenance action.

Source claim: subsetting bounds each client to typically 20-100 backends, with larger subsets when clients are fewer than backends or when client-side bursts concentrate load, and idle connections drop to UDP with reduced health checks. Inference: subset size trades assignment coverage against per-client memory and health-check load.

Source claim: random subsetting with 300 clients, 300 backends and a 30% subset gives the least-loaded backend 63% and the most-loaded 121% of average load; at 10% the range is 50-150%; roughly 75% subsets would be needed for even spread. Inference: these are simulation results rather than measurements, and they disqualify random selection at practical subset sizes.

Source claim: deterministic subsetting groups clients into rounds sharing a seeded shuffle, assigns each backend once per round and uses a different seed per round; the shuffle matters because ordered task updates would otherwise put consecutively updated backends into one subset. Inference: the round index makes assignment reproducible without coordination, and per-round seeds spread a failed backend's load beyond its subset.

Source claim: Round Robin can spread CPU up to 2x because of small subsets, varying query cost, machine diversity and unpredictable factors; the costliest requests may consume 1000x the cheapest, motivating pagination or functional caps. Inference: request-cost variance, not scheduling order, dominates the imbalance, and the proposed remedy changes the interface contract rather than the balancer.

Source claim: GCUs normalize heterogeneous CPU capacity; antagonistic neighbors produced performance differences up to 20%, and restarted tasks need minutes of warmup, so servers are prewarmed in lame duck. Inference: static capacity units cannot capture noisy-neighbor and JIT effects, so the scheduler needs runtime feedback, not only provisioning-time equivalence factors.

Source claim: Least-Loaded Round Robin filters to minimum active requests, but active-request counts are a poor capability proxy when requests block on I/O, each client sees only its own requests, and a fast-failing unhealthy task can sinkhole traffic; counting recent errors as active requests fixes that. Inference: the fix promotes error rate to a routing signal and requires a defined error taxonomy to avoid penalizing legitimate fast failures.

Source claim: Weighted Round Robin has backends report QPS, error rates and utilization in every response including health checks; clients adjust capability scores and penalize failures, and the measured CPU spread narrowed after switching. Inference: closing the loop on backend self-report makes routing depend on trustworthy, versioned feedback rather than on client-observable latency alone.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add the sinkhole failure (fast errors attract least-loaded traffic) and the active-request-versus-capability gap to the selection comparison.
Use the lame duck protocol (broadcast to active clients, UDP health checks to idle ones, 10-150 s grace) as the concrete drain contract behind the generic procedure.
Contrast deterministic subsetting rounds with shuffle shards: both bound the peer set, but only one is designed around overlap between tenants.
Classify the per-connection active-request cap as crude flow control with a documented backfire mode, distinct from admission control at the service edge.
Price reserved-but-unusable capacity: the 1,000-reserved/700-usable example treats load imbalance as idle headroom with a latency rationale.

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: Distributed Periodic Scheduling with Cron Service
readings.revision: Public SRE book chapter (sre.google web edition); retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 180 lines / 4555 words; six H2 sections (Cron; Cron Jobs and Idempotency; Cron at Large Scale; Building Cron at Google; The Roles of the Leader and the Follower; Summary); chrome excluded (lines 1-5 Jina title, URL and 'Markdown Content' header). Byline and editor lines 6-8 and footnotes 114-115 (lines 178-180) retained. Heading structure is flat: log compaction, snapshot/log storage and thundering-herd material sit under 'The Roles of the Leader and the Follower'.
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. The 2015 ACM Queue original named in footnote 114 was not fetched; bibliography entries (Ver15, Lam06) and footnote 115 target were not fetched; no Borg, Paxos or cron implementation was inspected.
sections: The Roles of the Leader and the Follower
notes: Source claim: traditional crond has a single-machine failure domain, persists only the crontab, and launches jobs fire-and-forget; anacron is the exception that relaunches missed daily-or-less-frequent jobs from a last-run timestamp. Inference: without a durable launch record, no distributed design can distinguish a missed launch from an unobserved one.

Source claim: jobs differ in idempotency (garbage collection versus a newsletter) and in whether a missed launch is acceptable (every five minutes versus monthly payroll); Google prefers skipping to double launching and fails closed. Inference: this is a stated policy default, not a correctness result, and the chapter says no single answer fits every job.

Source claim: a single cron machine in a 1,000-machine datacenter makes 1/1000 of capacity a single point of failure; decoupling processes from machines turns launches into scheduler RPCs, but rescheduling takes health-check timeouts plus install and start time, can lose local state, and can exceed the one-minute interval, so hot spares shorten the window. Inference: scheduler recovery latency, not cron logic, sets the shortest safe period and cron's availability bound.

Source claim: datacenter deployment uses containers and requires resource quantities up front, so a job may be delayed when capacity is unavailable, and launch state must be tracked from scheduled time to termination. Inference: admission delay is a normal scheduling outcome that the state model must represent, not an error to retry.

Source claim: a launch may need multiple RPCs and some may succeed while others fail, for example when the sending process dies mid-sequence. Inference: a logical launch is a non-atomic transaction spanning the cron log and the external scheduler, so recovery must reconcile partial effects.

Source claim: state is kept inside the cron service rather than external distributed storage because small writes are expensive on GFS/HDFS and base services should have few dependencies. Inference: the choice trades dependency risk for the burden of implementing replication, snapshots and restore inside the service.

Source claim: multiple replicas use Paxos; the leader is the only replica that writes state and launches jobs, the Fast Paxos leader doubles as cron leader, and failover stays within about one minute. Inference: single-writer authority simplifies mutual exclusion with the scheduler but makes failover latency a correctness parameter rather than an operational metric.

Source claim: launch start and completion are recorded synchronously through Paxos before and after the launch, and the start time uniquely identifies a launch, otherwise a new leader may repeat it. Inference: operation identity must include the scheduled time, not only the job name, or high-frequency jobs become ambiguous.

Source claim: a leader that loses leadership must immediately stop interacting with the datacenter scheduler to preserve mutual exclusion, and followers track state to take over. Inference: this is fencing by self-denial, which depends on the old leader learning of its demotion; the chapter does not fully examine a partition in which it does not.

Source claim: recovery requires either idempotent external operations or the ability to look up their state; precomputed job names let a new leader launch only missing names, and the scheduled time must be part of the name so a long failover cannot cause a second launch. Inference: naming is used as an idempotency key for the external scheduler, and the long-failover example shows why the key needs the scheduled time.

Source claim: the Paxos log is compacted by snapshots; snapshots are critical, stored locally and backed up to a distributed filesystem, while logs stay on local disk across three replicas with bounded loss accepted; a fresh replica can fetch snapshot and logs from a running peer. Inference: the recovery point is the last snapshot plus surviving logs, so the snapshot interval sets worst-case replay and loss.

Source claim: cron load is spiky; a '?' crontab field lets the system hash the job configuration over the time range to spread launches, yet spikes persist from jobs pinned to external events. Inference: jitter removes synchronization but not event-driven demand, so the herd problem is only partly mitigated.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add single-writer launch authority and the requirement that a demoted leader stop issuing external commands, as a concrete fencing obligation.
Use the one-minute failover budget and the resolution of open launches as constraints for leader-change acceptance tests.
Use the scheduled launch time in the external job name as the operation identity that prevents a double launch after an ambiguous RPC.
Anchor the missed-versus-duplicate launch policy and the definition-plus-interval run key to the cron chapter's fail-closed default and launch-time identity.
Distinguish snapshot backup from log retention: losing logs is bounded replay loss, losing snapshots is total state loss, which reframes the backup interval as a recovery objective.
Require cron replicas across diverse power domains and treat the datacenter scheduler as a shared-fate dependency of the scheduler service.

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: Shuffle Sharding: Massive and Magical Fault Isolation | Amazon Web Services
readings.revision: Public SRE book chapter, AWS article or PostgreSQL 18 docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed
readings.coverage: All 80 lines / 1591 words; sections Traditional Horizontal Scaling, Sharding and Bulkheads, Shuffle Sharding, Infima and Shuffle Sharding, Post-script; chrome excluded (extract contains no site navigation, cookie banner or footer links; only the trailing 'About the authors' heading is present with no bio text, and four figures exist as image URLs without transcribed captions)
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Four figure images not opened or described. No AWS documentation or Infima library documentation consulted; service-name claims taken from the article only.
notes: Representation: the file is a Jina reader rendering with a four-field header (Title, URL Source, Published Time, Markdown Content); body runs from line 8 to line 76 with a trailing author-bio heading at line 80 that carries no text.

Source claim (line 14, 42): shuffle sharding combines the rapidly diminishing overlap probability of dealt card hands with horizontal scaling, so that request-borne faults are confined to few instances.

Source claim (lines 18-22): traditional horizontal scaling spreads every request across all instances, so a single harmful or poisonous request can affect every instance; per-customer throttling can itself be overwhelmed.

Source claim (lines 26-34): dividing eight instances into four shards of two bounds a request-caused incident to roughly one quarter of customers, with the shard key chosen by customer id, operation type, resource id or a multidimensional combination.

Source claim (lines 46-54): two-of-eight shuffle shards give 56 potential shards (~1/56 impact); four-of-eight with three retries gives ~1/1680 impact; the article attributes the gain to client retry across every endpoint in the shard.

Arithmetic observation (inference, not a source claim): C(8,2)=28 and C(8,4)=70, whereas 56 and 1680 equal ordered selections P(8,2) and P(8,4). Distinct shard sets are therefore half and 1/24 of the quoted counts.

Source claim (line 76): the author's postscript corrects an earlier hand-count figure, replacing a permutations-based 7 million with a combinations-based 300,000 - the same permutations-vs-combinations distinction the shard counts in the body do not apply.

Source claim (lines 48-50): overlap between shuffle shards is acceptable because a fault-tolerant client retries each endpoint until one succeeds; impact is then bounded by the number of shards, not by instance count alone.

Source claim (line 58): stateless shuffle sharding hashes identifiers (compared to a bloom filter) and tolerates probabilistic overlap, while stateful searching shuffle sharding checks each new shard against all previously assigned shards to bound overlap explicitly.
Source claim (line 62): compartmentalization awareness lets shards draw a fixed number of endpoints per availability zone rather than purely at random, so zone placement is preserved inside a shard.

Source claim (lines 70-72): the general principles are many small units (cheaper capacity buffers, small contention impact) and partial membership overlap in exchange for an exponential increase in supported shards; the technique is offered as general-purpose for queues, rate limiters and locks.

Inference: the 1/56 and 1/1680 fractions assume failures confined to individual instances and retries that succeed elsewhere; correlated failure (shared dependency, zone-wide event) is not modelled, so realised isolation is weaker than the arithmetic suggests. 'Route 53 Infima' and 'RubberTrees' are managed-service names and only the technique is portable.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Bulkheads and retries as separate responsibilities; add shuffle-sharded endpoint assignment as a containment pattern whose effect depends on client retry behaviour.
Contrast disjoint shard sets with overlapping shuffle shards and state the combinatorial overlap budget as a distinct strategy family.
Per-tenant shard assignment as a placement axis: isolation strength versus instance count, including per-tenant DNS as an addressing consequence.
Noisy-neighbour containment: how partial overlap trades buffered capacity for a reduced blast radius, and where the scaling laws stop applying.
Limit of adding replicas: horizontal scaling does not isolate request-triggered faults, motivating shard membership rather than instance count.

readings.unit: Complete page or bounded chapter set: Chapter 11. Indexes
readings.revision: Public SRE book chapter, AWS article or PostgreSQL 18 docs; retrieved 2026-10-24; no immutable revision exposed (page titles identify PostgreSQL 18.6; the 'current' URL is mutable)
readings.coverage: All 601 lines / 9509 words; bounded chapter set of 13 blocks - chapter 11 landing page plus sections 11.1-11.12 concatenated, each block carrying its own Title/URL Source/Published Time header; chrome excluded (site header navigation, release banner, supported/development/unsupported version selector, prev/up/next pager table, submit-correction and policy footer appear only in the landing block; section blocks begin directly at body text)
readings.omissions: Linked docs/code not read; no execution. Chapter 14, 19.7, 24.1, 27.2, 65.x, 66.7, 5.12 and the bibliography entries referenced inline were not retrieved. No server was queried and no index was built, so no plan or timing was observed.
sections: 11.2 Index Types (11.2.1 B-Tree, 11.2.2 Hash, 11.2.3 GiST, 11.2.4 SP-GiST, 11.2.5 GIN, 11.2.6 BRIN)
notes: Representation: 13 concatenated reader captures; each begins with Title/URL Source/Published Time and 'Markdown Content'. The 'Published Time' value is identical (2026-08-13T12:52:54) across all blocks, so it is a fetch artefact rather than a document revision date - the docs are identified as PostgreSQL 18.6 in page titles and the 18 version row.
Source claim (11.9, line 421): all PostgreSQL indexes are secondary, stored separately from the table heap, so an ordinary index scan pays index access plus random heap access.

Source claim (11.9, lines 423-439): index-only scans require an index type that stores or can reconstruct values (B-tree always; GiST/SP-GiST only for some operator classes; GIN never) and a query referencing only stored columns, plus an all-visible visibility-map bit; without the bit a heap visit is still required and the advantage disappears.

Source claim (11.2, lines 113-127): B-tree is the default and serves =, <, <=, >=, >, BETWEEN, IN and IS NULL, can deliver sorted output, and helps LIKE/~ only for constant patterns anchored at the start, requiring pattern operator classes outside the C locale.

Source claim (11.3, lines 201-203): multicolumn B-tree efficiency depends on constraints on leading columns; the skip scan optimisation can apply later-column constraints by generating internal equality constraints, but only when the leading column has few distinct values.

Source claim (11.5, line 250): combining indexes builds in-memory bitmaps, ANDs/ORs them and visits heap rows in physical order, losing index ordering and adding per-index scan cost, so the planner sometimes prefers a single index scan.

Source claim (11.8, line 371): a partial index is usable only if the planner can prove the query's WHERE mathematically implies the predicate; matching happens at plan time, so parameterized clauses such as 'x < ?' never qualify, and PostgreSQL is explicitly not a theorem prover for equivalent forms.

Source claim (11.8, lines 397-411): a family of non-overlapping partial indexes keyed by category is a bad substitute for partitioning because the planner must test each index; a single leading-column index or declared partitioning is preferred.

Source claim (11.9, lines 453-459): INCLUDE payload columns are not search-key columns, need not be indexable types, do not participate in uniqueness, and are supported only for B-tree, GiST and SP-GiST; wide payload columns risk tuple-size failures and bloat.

Source claim (11.1 line 103; 11.1 line 105): building an index on a large table permits concurrent reads but blocks writes unless CONCURRENTLY is used (with caveats); indexes add write overhead and prevent heap-only tuple updates, so unused indexes should be dropped.

Source claim (11.12, lines 585-599): index-usage analysis requires ANALYZE first, real data volumes (a 1-in-100 selection is a poor candidate because it fits one page), and forced-plan experiments with enable_seqscan/enable_nestloop before blaming cost estimates.

Inference: the chapter's guidance presumes reasonably stable value distributions and offers no measurement protocol for skewed, seasonal or rapidly changing workloads; the small-test-data warning is qualitative, with no sample-size rule.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Anchor access-path choices in index type capability (operator class, sort order, uniqueness) rather than in generic 'add an index' advice.
Plan-time predicate implication for partial indexes, and why prepared/parameterized statements cannot use them, as a selectivity-model limit.
Index lifecycle cost: write amplification, HOT blocking, blocking versus concurrent build, and removal of unused indexes as a lifecycle stage.
Visibility-map freshness as the precondition for index-only scans links vacuum state to read-path performance, not only to space reclamation.
Index creation as a DDL budget item: lock profile of a default build versus CONCURRENTLY, and the caveats that make concurrent builds unsuitable for some migrations.

readings.revision: OASIS SOA-RM v1.0; retrieved 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: All 655 lines / 10451 words; §1-5 (1.1-1.6, 2.1-2.3, 3.1-3.3 incl. 3.2.1-3.2.3 and 3.3.1-3.3.3), glossary entries and committee list; Jina header and empty-anchor chrome excluded

sections: 1.2 A Reference Model for Service Oriented Architectures
1.4 Guide to using the reference model
2.1 What is Service Oriented Architecture? (§2 heading absent)
2.1.1 A worked Service Oriented Architecture example
2.2 How is Service Oriented Architecture different?
2.3 The Benefits of Service Oriented Architecture
notes: Source claim: SOA is 'a paradigm for organizing and utilizing distributed capabilities that may be under the control of different ownership domains' (line 93; glossary line 575). Inference: ownership boundaries, not transport or granularity, are the model's organizing axis; that is compatible with Tycho's boundary decisions but is an application, not a statement of the source.

Source claim: a reference model is independent of specific standards, technologies, implementations and concrete details (line 12), and Web services are 'too solution specific to be part of a general reference model' (line 129). Inference: citing this source cannot support claims about SOAP/REST, message buses or deployment shape.

Source claim: reference model, reference architecture and concrete architecture are separated by abstraction level, illustrated through housing (lines 12-22). Inference: the glossary entry for reference architecture (line 541) is narrower than the housing illustration; the text does not fully reconcile the two, so neither should be quoted as a settled taxonomy.

Source claim: visibility is satisfied when participants can interact; awareness, willingness and reachability are preconditions stated with MUST in places (lines 217-243). Inference: these are necessary conditions for interaction, not guarantees or measurable criteria; a book test must operationalize them independently.

Source claim: 'loose coupling' and 'coarse-grained' are intentionally not used because they are subjective trade-offs without useful metrics (line 127). Inference: the source rejects those labels as design criteria; Tycho's measured-boundary framing is a different basis and should not be presented as the source's method.

Source claim: a service is opaque, exposing only interface information and suitability information (line 189); descriptions SHOULD use a standard referenceable format (line 351) and required detail may be included by reference (line 361). Inference: description is broader than an interface schema, but the model specifies no description language or registry protocol.

notes: Source claim: Citus is a PostgreSQL extension that lets commodity servers ('nodes') coordinate in a 'shared nothing' architecture, forming a cluster that can hold more data and use more CPU cores than one computer, scaling by adding nodes (line 10). Inference: this is a vendor scale-out claim without measurements, hardware assumptions or workload definitions.

Source claim: every cluster has one coordinator; applications send queries there, and it either routes each query to one worker or parallelizes it across several according to metadata tables tracking worker DNS names, health and data distribution (lines 12-16). Inference: the coordinator is both entry point and routing-metadata authority, so it sits on the query critical path; the page does not discuss coordinator failover.

Source claim: row-based sharding uses a shared schema and a distribution column, requires every table to carry that column and every query to filter by it, and suits IoT workloads and hardware efficiency (lines 24-42). Inference: the page presents these as design requirements and benefits, not measured results; 'best performance' is unqualified.

Source claim: schema-based sharding (Citus 12.0+) makes the schema the logical shard, requires no query changes beyond setting search_path, allows heterogeneous tenant schemas, and supports fewer tenants per node (lines 44-60). Inference: the model shifts isolation to schema permissions and gives up parallel cross-tenant queries according to the table at line 72.

Source claim: the tradeoff table gives 1-10k tenants for schema-based and 1-1M+ for row-based sharding, and marks parallel cross-tenant queries 'No' for schema-based and 'Yes' for row-based (lines 64-76). Inference: the ranges have no stated methodology, node size or data volume, so they are orientation, not capacity limits.

Source claim: the page says 'There are three types of tables' (line 82) and then enumerates five — distributed, reference, local, local managed and schema (lines 84-122). Inference: the count and the enumeration disagree; the enumeration should be cited and the inconsistency preserved rather than silently reconciled.

Source claim: distributed tables look normal to SQL but are horizontally partitioned; DDL cascades to shards; the administrator chooses a distribution column and rows are assigned deterministically by hashing its value (lines 86-98). Inference: determinism does not imply even distribution; skew is deferred to a linked data-modeling page not read.

Source claim: a reference table's entire contents sit in one shard replicated on every worker, have no distribution column, and writes use two-phase commit (lines 100-106). Inference: this trades write coordination and per-worker storage for local reads; the page quantifies neither.

Source claim: pg_dist_shard holds one row per shard with a hash-space range; the example has four shards; shard count is configurable per table at distribution time; placement is resolved by joining pg_dist_placement and pg_dist_node (lines 124-163). Inference: routing depends on metadata indirection, and this text ties shard count to creation time, which bears on later resharding that the page does not describe.

Source claim: shards can be replicated with PostgreSQL streaming replication, described as transparent and not requiring Citus metadata tables (line 165). Inference: Citus routing metadata therefore does not itself track replica state per this page; failover behavior is outside the unit.

Source claim: the rendered title is 'Concepts - Citus 13.0.1 documentation' while the URL path is /en/stable/ (lines 1-3). Inference: 13.0.1 is a version marker, but 'stable' is a moving alias, so the retrieved page is live documentation rather than an immutable edition.

Source claim: multi-shard queries become per-shard tasks queued for worker connections; each session has a pool, capped per worker by citus.max_adaptive_executor_pool_size, with slow-start interval, cached idle connections and max_shared_pool_size as a fail-safe (lines 183-199). Inference: connection behavior is adaptive and per session, so tuning depends on workload; the linked tuning page was not read.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Candidate anchor for a two-model sharding taxonomy: row-based (shared schema, distribution column required in every table and query) versus schema-based (schema as logical shard since 12.0), with the page's tenant ranges and cross-tenant parallelism column as source claims to qualify.

Candidate anchor for the shard-key constraint: assignment is deterministic by hashing the distribution column and row-based queries must include it; the page offers no skew measurement, so it can support the constraint but not hotspot evidence.

Candidate anchor for why shard count is a creation-time decision: the page says it is configurable per table at distribution time and routing reads fixed hash ranges from pg_dist_shard; it does not describe moving or splitting shards.

Candidate example of read locality versus write coordination: reference tables are fully replicated to every worker and writes use two-phase commit; the page states a consistency intent but gives no failure or latency analysis.

Candidate for testing scale-out claims: the page asserts more nodes add data capacity and CPU and that fragmenting one query raises parallelism, while noting results return through the coordinator; it reports no throughput or speedup measurements.
