Source claim: a metric is a measurement of a service captured at runtime, and a metric event consists of the measurement plus its capture time and associated metadata (1005). Inference: the definition is event-shaped, but the rest of the page describes aggregate instruments and exported data points rather than individual events.

Source claim: application and request metrics indicate availability and performance; custom metrics can connect availability to user experience or the business; collected data can alert on an outage or trigger autoscaling (1007). Inference: the autoscaling claim is a use case, not a control-loop design, and the page supplies no thresholds or feedback analysis.

Source claim: a Meter Provider is a factory for Meters, initialized once with a lifecycle matching the application and including Resource and Exporter setup; some SDKs provide a global provider (1013). A Meter creates instruments (1017), and a Metric Exporter sends data to stdout, the Collector or a vendor backend (1021). Inference: shutdown, flush and multi-provider behavior are absent.

Source claim: an instrument is defined by name, kind and optional unit and description, with names and units chosen by the developer or taken from semantic conventions (1025-1032). Kinds are Counter, Asynchronous Counter, UpDownCounter, Asynchronous UpDownCounter, Gauge, Asynchronous Gauge and Histogram, with odometer, queue-length and fuel-gauge analogies (1036-1042). Inference: only Gauge is explicitly called synchronous; whether the other non-asynchronous kinds are synchronous is left implicit.

Source claim: aggregation combines many measurements into exact or estimated statistics over a time window; OTLP transports aggregated metrics; each instrument has a default aggregation that Views can override (1048). Inference: 'estimated' acknowledges histogram approximation but the page gives no error bounds or bucket guidance.

Source claim: metrics are intended to provide statistical aggregate information, unlike request tracing which captures request lifecycles (1050). The use-case list includes bytes by protocol, bytes per request, system-call duration, request-size trends, CPU or memory usage, average balance values and active requests (1052-1058). Inference: the list mixes counter, gauge and histogram shapes without mapping them, and 'average balance' is business data whose privacy implications the page does not address.

Source claim: cardinality is the number of unique attribute combinations; the SDK keeps a separate aggregation state (data point) per combination, so memory scales with combinations rather than request volume, and high-cardinality attributes such as user IDs or raw URL paths can cause unbounded growth (1066). The default limit is 2000 and can be overridden with a View (1068). Inference: the default is presented as SDK-wide without a spec version, so conformance should be checked per implementation.

Source claim: at the limit, additional combinations are not dropped outright; measurements are folded into a single overflow data point marked otel.metric.overflow=true, so no measurements are lost, memory is bounded, and the marker is common across SDKs, languages and backends (1070-1074). Inference: this is a specific, testable conformance claim that the page does not evidence with an implementation matrix.

Source claim: queries that filter or group by any attribute undercount after overflow because the entire attribute combination is replaced, not just the high-cardinality part; the worked example shows success=false being dropped along with url.path, so an error-rate alert can stop firing while the total stays correct (1076-1078). Inference: this is the page's most consequential operational warning and deserves explicit treatment wherever metric alerts are designed.

Source claim: the limit applies only to attributes supplied through the metrics API; Resource attributes such as service.name and instrumentation-scope attributes are not limited and remain on every data point including overflow (1082-1087). The page warns that this is not a reason to relocate measurement attributes and gives an entity/scope/measurement modeling rule (1087). Inference: the guidance is architectural rather than normative API text.

Source claim: for synchronous instruments, delta temporality resets state each cycle so the limit bounds only combinations active in one cycle, while cumulative temporality retains state so new combinations keep overflowing until the process restarts; asynchronous instruments differ and are out of scope (1091-1096). Inference: long-lived cumulative processes can saturate permanently after 2000 combinations, but the page offers no restart or mitigation advice.

Source claim: a log is a timestamped text record, either structured (recommended) or unstructured, with optional metadata; logs have the biggest legacy of the signals and most languages already have logging facilities (1011). Source claim: OpenTelemetry provides a Logs API and SDK for log records plus language SDKs and bridges; logs are anything sent through a Logging Provider, and events are a special type of logs such that all events are logs but not all logs are events (1015). Inference: this is a definitional taxonomy without a formal event schema, although EventName later appears as a log-record field (1215).

Source claim: OpenTelemetry is designed to work with existing logs, correlate them with other signals, add contextual attributes and normalize sources (1017). The Collector supplies receivers, filelogreceiver, transformprocessor and exporters to non-OpenTelemetry formats (1021-1026), and deploying a Collector as a general-purpose logging agent is frequently the first adoption step (1028). Inference: this is adoption guidance without measured cost or migration effort.

Source claim: application logs are created with any logging library; with autoinstrumentation or an SDK, OpenTelemetry automatically correlates existing logs with the active trace and span, wrapping the log body with their IDs (1032). Inference: 'wrapping the log body' conflicts with the top-level TraceId and SpanId fields listed later (1206-1207); the page does not clarify body injection versus field assignment.

Source claim: JSON is not automatically structured; a structured log has a defined, consistent schema or typed fields that downstream systems can parse, and the textual encoding may be JSON, protobuf or another format (1054-1058). Common Log Format and CLF-plus-JSON hybrid examples are given, with filelogreceiver helpers for mixed formats (1097-1109). Inference: schema stability, not encoding, is the criterion, but no schema registry or enforcement mechanism is named.

Source claim: unstructured logs are human-readable and common in development but not preferred for production because parsing at scale needs regular expressions and custom parsers (1115-1127); semistructured logs have machine-readable key/value or delimited fields but no stable schema across emitters and may need mapping and type coercion (1129-1139). Inference: the three categories are presented as covering any log format, but the boundaries are judgment calls rather than formal tests.

sections: What should OTel Baggage be used for? (1010-1016)
Baggage is not the same as attributes (1023-1031)
notes: Coverage claim: the substantive body is only lines 993-1031, 488 words including headings and two image links, against 1063 lines and 6183 words for the whole representation; chrome is 5695 words, about 92 percent. Inference: this page is a short concept note wrapped in the site template, and its body should be quoted as a whole rather than sampled.

Source claim: baggage is contextual information that resides next to context; it is a key-value store that lets you propagate any data alongside context (995-997). Inference: 'any data' is unbounded on this page, with no size, type or count limit stated.

Source claim: baggage lets data cross services and processes and be available to add to traces, metrics or logs in those services (999). Inference: availability is not automatic attachment; the later attributes section confirms that baggage must be read and added explicitly.

Source claim: the example starts with a clientId at request start and wants it on all spans in a trace, some metrics in another service and some logs; context propagation carries the baggage and instrumentations automatically propagate baggage (1003-1007). Inference: automatic propagation concerns header flow, not conversion into telemetry attributes; the two SVG diagrams (1009, 1016) are present only as image links with alt text 'OTel Baggage'.

Source claim: baggage is best used for information typically available only at the start of a request and needed further downstream, such as account identification, user IDs, product IDs and origin IPs (1012); a user ID on a database span makes it easier to find which users see the slowest calls, and the same ID can appear in logs (1014). Inference: the examples are personal or tenant identifiers, which the later security section only partly addresses.

Source claim: automatic instrumentation includes baggage in most network requests; baggage and other trace-context parts are sent in HTTP headers and are visible to anyone inspecting network traffic; if traffic is restricted the risk may not apply, but downstream services could propagate baggage outside the network (1019). Inference: the risk model is boundary-dependent, and this page gives no filtering or allow-list mechanism.

Source claim: there are no built-in integrity checks to ensure baggage items are yours, so reading them requires caution (1021). Inference: this is an authenticity and integrity gap, not only confidentiality, and the page offers no verification recipe.

Source claim: baggage is a separate key-value store and is unassociated with attributes on spans, metrics or logs unless explicitly added; adding requires reading baggage and attaching values as attributes (1025-1027). Several languages provide Baggage Span Processors that add baggage data as span attributes at creation (1029). Inference: processor availability and behavior are language-specific and not listed.

Source claim: the page links the baggage specification for more information (1031) and the footer records last modified 2026-02-22 by commit 4b5381a2 (1044). Inference: wire format, size limits, propagation rules and normative security requirements are outside this unit; the live page may change after the 2026-10-24 capture.

Candidate anchor for the scope statement that untrusted baggage must not become an authorization decision; the source only says to exercise caution when reading (1021) and states no authorization rule.

Candidate anchor for sensitive baggage content: the source says baggage is visible to network inspectors and downstream services may propagate it outside the network (1019); the book page lists baggage, tracestate and attributes as leakage paths and proposes minimum-field correlation.

Candidate anchor for retention and access of propagated identifiers: the source's examples include user IDs, account IDs and origin IPs (1012); the book page owns minimization, redaction and cross-collection isolation, but not header propagation.

sections: Table Co-Location (68-211): hash-distributed co-location (74-82), practical example (84-103), regular PostgreSQL comparison (105-120), distributing by ID (122-162), distributing by tenant (164-193), feature support (195-211)
notes: Coverage claim: the page is nearly all prose and SQL examples, 2830 of 2844 words; only header, logo link and link-target syntax were excluded. The four diagrams are image links with alt text only (20, 80, 150, 189), so their visual content is outside the text representation. Inference: the page does not depend on the diagrams for its main argument, but a reader cannot verify the illustrated shard placement from this representation.

Source claim: the distribution column assigns table rows to shards and choosing it is 'one of the most important' modeling decisions; a correct choice groups related data on the same nodes, makes queries fast and supports all SQL features, while a wrong choice runs needlessly slowly and cannot support all SQL features across nodes (8-10). Inference: 'fast', 'slow' and 'all SQL features' are unqualified by workload, node count or measurement.

Source claim: multi-tenant modeling puts a tenant id on each table and routes a tenant-scoped query to the single worker holding that tenant's shard; best practices are to distribute by tenant_id, convert small cross-tenant tables to reference tables, and filter every application query by tenant_id (16-32). Inference: the routing benefit depends on every query carrying the tenant predicate; the page later admits tenant_id may need adding to unique constraints and join conditions (191).

Source claim: real-time modeling uses an entity id such as user, host or device; best practices are high cardinality, even distribution, distributing fact and dimension tables on common columns, and using reference tables for dimensions that cannot be co-located (38-50). Inference: cardinality and skew are not quantified, so the advice cannot be tested against a concrete key distribution from this page alone.

Source claim: using a timestamp as the distribution column is called the most common timeseries mistake because hash distribution scatters time and range queries then fan out; the recommendation is to distribute on tenant or entity id and use PostgreSQL table partitioning for time (56-64). Inference: the argument is specific to hash distribution; range distribution is not discussed on this page, so the conclusion should not be generalized to every distribution method.

Source claim: co-location means tables share a distribution column and shards with the same hash range stay on the same node, even after rebalance, so equal distribution-column values are on the same node across tables (70-78). Inference: this hash-range invariant carries the page's later SQL-feature claims; the rebalance guarantee is asserted but not demonstrated.

Source claim: the worked example distributes event by event_id and page by page_id, which forces two queries and application-side combination with per-shard overhead (124-160); distributing both by tenant_id with colocate_with => 'event' lets the original join run in one step on one node (164-191). Inference: the comparison is qualitative; no plan, latency, data volume or shard count is given.

Source claim: co-location unlocks full SQL on one co-located shard set, multi-statement transactions on that set, aggregation via INSERT..SELECT, foreign keys, distributed outer joins, and pushdown CTEs requiring PostgreSQL 12 or later (197-209). Inference: 'full list' is scoped to this page and version; features for queries spanning multiple shard sets are not enumerated here.

Source claim: Citus splits queries into fragment tasks that run on worker shards in parallel; a two-stage optimizer first rewrites queries into pushable commutative and associative form, then workers apply standard PostgreSQL planning to the fragments (215-219). Inference: the claim that performance is cumulative across cluster cores is a design argument, not a benchmark; the linked tuning page was not read.

Source claim: line 217 refers to choosing the right 'distribution method' as well as the right column, but the page only explains hash distribution (78). Inference: the unit covers column choice under hash distribution; range or other distribution methods are outside its text.

Revision claim: the rendered title says Citus 13.0.1 while the URL uses /en/stable/ (1-3). Inference: 'stable' is a moving alias, so this is live documentation and may change after the 2026-10-24 capture.

Candidate anchor for connecting distribution-column choice to skew: the source says a low-cardinality or skewed column concentrates work on some nodes (44-46); the book page's hot-tenant counterexample tests that risk without assuming even key load.

Candidate anchor for the creation-time constraint: the source fixes the column and co-location group in create_distributed_table (128-129, 171-172) and does not describe changing them; the book page owns moving ownership without conflicting writes.

Candidate anchor for the relational consequence: the source says tenant_id may need to appear in unique constraints and join conditions (191) and lists foreign keys and multi-statement transactions as co-location features (201-205); the book page owns constraint and isolation scope.

Candidate anchor for qualifying the performance claim: the source says parallel fragment tasks make throughput cumulative across cluster cores (215) and that the second planning phase is ordinary PostgreSQL behavior (219); the book page supplies conditional scaling models instead of vendor throughput assertions.

sections: High-importance producer settings: 14 entries, key.serializer through ssl.truststore.password (8-139)
Medium-importance producer settings: 46 entries, batch.size through ssl.truststore.type (140-641)
Low-importance producer settings: 52 entries, acks through transactional.id (642-1146)
notes: Coverage claim: this is a flat reference page with no introduction, worked example, navigation or footer; every one of the 112 entries has a name heading, description, and a Type/Default/Valid Values/Importance table. Inference: the importance tiers are editorial priority for typical use, not a statement about which settings interact; several correctness relationships have to be assembled across entries.

Structure claim: key.serializer and value.serializer lead the high tier, and the remaining entries are alphabetical within each tier (high 14, medium 46, low 52). Inference: the ordering is a lookup convention, not a dependency order; entries such as retries, acks, enable.idempotence and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection constrain one another only through their descriptions.

Source claim: bootstrap.servers is a host:port list with default '' and need not contain all brokers; buffer.memory defaults to 33554432 bytes and must cover records waiting to be sent, blocking for max.block.ms before failing; compression.type defaults to none with valid values none, gzip, snappy, lz4 and zstd (26-48). Inference: buffer.memory is explicitly not a hard memory bound because compression and in-flight requests use additional memory (39).

Source claim: retries defaults to 2147483647; a value above zero is required for idempotence; zero disables automatic retry and surfaces transient errors; the page recommends leaving it unset and controlling retry behavior with delivery.timeout.ms; with idempotence false and more than one in-flight request, retries can reorder records (55-61). Inference: the numerical default is effectively bounded by the delivery deadline, not by the retry count.

Source claim: batch.size defaults to 16384 bytes and zero disables batching; linger.ms defaults to 5 and adds up to that delay waiting for more records; both entries note the default changed from 0 to 5 in Apache Kafka 4.0, and broker backpressure can raise effective linger time (140-150, 220-228). Inference: batching and latency defaults are version-specific, so pre-4.0 tuning advice does not carry over unchanged.

Source claim: delivery.timeout.ms defaults to 120000 ms as an upper bound after send() returns, covering delay, acknowledgement wait and retriable failures, and should be at least request.timeout.ms plus linger.ms; max.block.ms defaults to 60000 ms and bounds send() metadata and buffer-allocation waits (211-219, 229-237). Inference: these form a deadline hierarchy, but the page states the recommended inequality without describing enforcement or validation.

Source claim: acks defaults to all and accepts all, -1, 0 and 1; 0 gives no server acknowledgement guarantee and disables retry knowledge, 1 can lose a record if the leader fails before replication, and all waits for the full in-sync replica set (642-650). Inference: the durability level is a producer setting only in combination with broker replication and ISR conditions, which this page does not define.

Source claim: enable.idempotence defaults to true and requires max.in.flight.requests.per.connection at most 5, retries above 0 and acks=all; conflicting settings disable idempotence when it was not explicitly enabled, while explicitly enabling it with conflicts throws ConfigException; max.in.flight.requests.per.connection defaults to 5 because the broker retains at most five batches per producer (657-661, 686-694). Inference: changing acks or retries can silently downgrade the default idempotence guarantee unless enable.idempotence is set explicitly.

Source claim: partitioner.class defaults to null; with no custom partitioner, a present key selects a partition by hash, otherwise records go to a sticky partition that changes after at least batch.size bytes; RoundRobinPartitioner has a known uneven-distribution issue (KAFKA-9965); partitioner.ignore.keys defaults false, adaptive partitioning defaults true and availability timeout defaults 0 (247-274, 772-783). Inference: partition assignment depends on key presence and accumulated bytes, so it is not a fixed mapping over time.

Source claim: transactional.id defaults to null; without it the producer is limited to idempotent delivery, and configuring it implies idempotence; transactions are recommended to require at least three brokers, adjustable through broker transaction.state.log.replication.factor; transaction.timeout.ms defaults to 60000 and a request above broker transaction.max.timeout.ms fails with InvalidTxnTimeoutException (1120-1146). Inference: transactional capability depends on cluster size and broker limits, not on the producer setting alone.

Source claim: 8 of the 14 high-importance entries are TLS key/truststore settings (ssl.key.password, ssl.keystore.certificate.chain, ssl.keystore.key, ssl.keystore.location, ssl.keystore.password, ssl.truststore.certificates, ssl.truststore.location, ssl.truststore.password) (68-139), while SASL and OAUTHBEARER settings occupy medium and low tiers (291-560, 826-1056). Inference: the tier label reflects broad client importance, not a security ranking; a secured deployment still has to read beyond the high tier.

Source claim: enable.metrics.push defaults to true and pushes client metrics when the cluster has a matching subscription; metric.reporters defaults to JmxReporter and metrics.recording.level to INFO (668-676, 731-762). Inference: client telemetry is on by default with no correctness role, so a restricted deployment must decide explicitly whether to keep it.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Candidate anchor for producer routing: the source's default partitioner hashes a present key and otherwise uses a sticky partition that changes after batch.size bytes (251-253); the book page argues that partition-key choice is a correctness and scaling choice, not a transparent optimization (83-89).

Candidate anchor for the durability setting: acks defaults to all in this Kafka 4.1 page (654), while the book page treats acks and min.insync.replicas as a trade-off whose guarantee also depends on ISR and leader election (53, 72-78).

Candidate anchor for the limits of idempotence and transactions: the source presents enable.idempotence and transactional.id as producer-side guarantees (657-661, 1138-1140); the book page states that neither encloses an unrelated database or external effect (71-86).

Candidate anchor for retry budgeting: the source recommends using delivery.timeout.ms rather than a retry count, with exponential retry backoff settings (57, 808-825); the book page requires a total absolute deadline and bounded attempt budget rather than an effectively unbounded retry default.

Candidate anchor for the batching latency trade-off: the source states that linger.ms adds up to 5 ms by default and broker backpressure can raise it (222); the book page owns critical-path and percentile reasoning, which the producer page does not connect to end-to-end latency.

Candidate anchor for choosing a delivery contract: the producer page describes acks=0/1/all and idempotence mechanics but does not compare durable work queues with retained logs; the book page starts from what a consumer must own before selecting a family (51-64).

sections: Persistence: Don't fear the filesystem; Constant Time Suffices (24-51)
Efficiency: message-set batching, common binary format, sendfile/zero-copy, TLS limitation, end-to-end batch compression (53-94)
The Producer: Load balancing; Asynchronous send (96-108)
The Consumer: Push vs. pull; Consumer Position; Offline Data Load; Static Membership (110-152)
Message Delivery Semantics: at-most/at-least/exactly once, idempotent producer, transactions, read_committed (154-181)
Using Transactions: transactional producer/consumer configuration, exception classes, reset policy (183-214)
Unheaded Kafka 4.1 share-groups preview: cooperative record consumption, acquisition locks, per-partition lock limit (216-240)
Replication: replicated logs, ISR/quorums, unclean leader election, availability/durability, replica management (242-320)
Log Compaction: basics, guarantees, details, configuring the log cleaner (322-412)
Quotas: necessity, client groups, configuration precedence, bandwidth/request-rate quotas, enforcement (414-458)
notes: Provenance: this record is against the corrected content page /41/design/design/ (460 lines / 11,878 words); the earlier /41/design/ item is a separate 217-line / 753-word section index with only two child links and no design prose. The content page has no site navigation or footer; the only chrome is the 4.1 banner and reader header.

Source claim (10-22): Kafka was designed as a unified platform for real-time feeds, with high throughput, backlog handling, low latency, partitioned processing and fault tolerance; the authors describe the result as closer to a database log than a traditional messaging system.

Source claim (28-51): Kafka relies on the filesystem and pagecache instead of an in-process cache; all data is written immediately to a persistent log, a 32GB machine can use 28-30GB as cache, and restart keeps the cache warm; log reads and appends are O(1), avoiding BTree O(log N) operations and 10ms disk seeks. Inference: these are design arguments, not measurements performed in this page.

Source claim (53-86): efficiency work targets small I/O and byte copying; message sets amortize round trips, producer/broker/consumer share a binary format, and sendfile avoids user-space copies. Kafka disables sendfile when TLS/SSL is enabled because the TLS library runs in user space. Inference: the zero-copy path is conditional, so the throughput rationale does not apply unchanged to encrypted links.

Source claim (88-94): batch compression is end-to-end; the broker decompresses a batch to validate it (for example, record count against the header), then stores and forwards it compressed; GZIP, Snappy, LZ4 and Zstandard are supported. Inference: broker validation still costs decompression CPU, so compression saves network and disk rather than all broker work.

Source claim (98-122): producers send directly to the partition leader after metadata lookup and choose partitions randomly or by a key hash; consumers pull with an offset, can rewind, and use long-poll parameters to avoid busy-waiting. The authors reject an end-to-end pull/store-and-forward producer design because thousands of producers and disks would be an operational burden.

Source claim (126-152): broker-side per-message acknowledgement state is replaced by one committed offset per partition per consumer group, checkpointed periodically and rewindable; this makes acknowledgement cheap but makes replay an expected capability. Static membership adds persistent group instance IDs so administrative restarts do not trigger rebalances; duplicate IDs are fenced with FencedInstanceIdException.

Source claim (154-181): delivery is at-most-once, at-least-once or exactly-once; a message is committed when all in-sync replicas apply it; pre-0.11 resends could duplicate, while 0.11 adds an idempotent producer (producer ID plus sequence) and transactions across partitions. Consumer order of save/process selects at-most-once versus at-least-once; exactly-once is available inside Kafka read-process-write with read_committed, while external destinations require their own cooperation or two-phase commit.

Source claim (183-214): only the producer is transactional, but it can commit consumer offsets in the same transaction; the recommended setup is one producer per consumer, isolation.level=read_committed and enable.auto.commit=false, with transactional.id fencing a restarted instance. AbortableException requires abort plus explicit consumer-position reset; the page lists six exception categories and offers discard-and-recreate as a simple policy.

Source claim (216-240): Kafka 4.1 previews share groups, where partitions may be assigned to multiple consumers, records are acknowledged individually, delivery attempts are counted, and a time-limited acquisition lock (default 30s) plus group.share.partition.max.record.locks bounds in-flight records. Inference: this is a distinct consumption contract, not a configuration of traditional consumer groups; the representation gives it no heading.

Source claim (242-320): replication uses one leader and followers per partition; liveness requires a controller session and sufficient replication progress; the ISR is persisted, any ISR member is electable, and a write is committed only after all ISR members receive it. Kafka chooses ISR over majority quorum to tolerate f failures with f+1 replicas; unclean leader election is off by default since 0.11; acks=0/1/all and min.insync.replicas set the producer/durability trade-off. Inference: this page's ISR-only election wording does not include the later Eligible Leader Replicas rules cited on the book's replication page.

Source claim (322-458): log compaction retains at least the last value per key using background recopy, stable offsets and tombstones (delete markers expire after delete.retention.ms, default 24h); quotas limit per-client bandwidth and request-thread time, with eight-level precedence and broker-side delay plus channel muting. Inference: compaction changes what replay can reconstruct, and quotas protect broker capacity rather than isolating tenant data or authorization.

tycho_candidates.candidate: The page's partition-ordering question already uses the design's Producer/Load balancing and Consumer/Consumer Position sections (65-89); add the source's direct-to-leader routing, metadata lookup, single-integer consumer offset, pull plus long poll, and rewind capability, while keeping the page's warning that partition order is not topic-wide order.

The page cites the design's Replication section but adds Eligible Leader Replicas from the operations page (53, 72-80); reconcile the design's ISR-only election and all-ISR commit wording (290-314) with that ELR caveat, and do not read this design page as covering ELR.

The page already links the design page for delivery semantics and transactions (73, 85); add the source's exact scope: producer-ID/sequence deduplication, read_committed visibility, transactional.id, and the statement that external destinations need cooperation (168-181, 197-201). Preserve the page's conclusion that a Kafka transaction does not enclose a SQL or payment effect.

The chapter ledger E02 records only five design sections as inspected (100-104); update it against the full ten-section page, including Persistence, Efficiency, Log Compaction, Quotas and the 4.1 share-groups preview, or state explicitly why those sections remain outside the claim scope.

The source scopes exactly-once delivery to Kafka read-process-write and says other destination systems generally require cooperation (177-181); use that sentence to qualify the outbox page's statement that broker producer idempotence or transactions cannot make an unrelated consumer's external effect globally exactly once (167, 231).

sections: Definition, Workflow step versus Standalone Activity, Activity Task Execution (12-14)
Define an Activity function; SDK examples (16-30)
Idempotency: motivation, replay/retry edge case, idempotency keys, granularity (32-71)
Activity retry policy: durable backoff, start_to_close timeout, observed-once completion, manual-retry caution (73-81)
Activity parameters: arguments and return values in Event History (83-85)
Activity Type: name versus function/method/class reference (87-89)
Register the Activity with a Worker: Task Queue, name mapping, Workflow and Standalone starts (91-110)
Best practices for defining Activities: serialization, idempotent writes, timeouts, heartbeats (112-119)
notes: Source claim (12-14): an Activity Definition is a normal function or method that executes one well-defined action; once registered with a Worker it can be started as a Workflow step or as a Standalone Activity, and it gives rise to an Activity Task Execution. Inference: definition (code), type (name) and execution (attempt) are distinct levels that the page separates later.

Source claim (16-30): examples exist for Go, Java, PHP, Python, TypeScript, .NET and Rust; the captured representation contains only the Go sample, `func YourSimpleActivity(ctx context.Context) error`. The other language tabs are present as labels but their code panels are not in this representation; no section is missing.

Source claim (32-51): Temporal recommends idempotent Activities; idempotence means repeated execution has the same result, with infrastructure-as-code provisioning and payment charging as examples. Activities are an atomic unit of execution and either complete or not; lack of idempotence can affect application correctness but does not cause a platform error.

Source claim (41): completed Activities do not re-execute during Workflow Replay, but an Activity is not recorded in Event History until it returns or errors; if the Worker crashes after success but before reporting, the Activity is retried. Inference: exactly-once history observation and at-least-once execution are compatible, so effect identity must survive an ambiguous completion.

Source claim (53-67): a three-step Activity (database lookup, microservice call, filesystem write) replays all three steps on retry; splitting it into three Activities narrows replay but grows Event History. Idempotency keys are enforced by the downstream service, and Workflow Run ID plus Activity ID is offered as a stable key across retries and unique across Workflow Executions.

Source claim (73-81): the retry mechanism provides durable execution and tracks exponential backoff even if a Worker crashes; start_to_close timeout is how the platform detects an inactive Activity. Temporal guarantees the Activity is observed as completed exactly once, but it may execute multiple times and may partially complete more than once. The page cautions against manual retry logic inside the Activity.

Source claim (83-89): function or method parameters and return values are recorded in the Workflow Execution's Event History; an Activity Type is a name that can identify the definition when starting an Activity, alternatively a function/method/class reference.

Source claim (91-110): an Activity Definition does not run until a Worker registers it and polls the Task Queue; registration maps the Activity Type name to the function, so callers can start by name without a code reference. One Worker can register many Activities, and one registration serves both Workflow and Standalone starts; Go and TypeScript can set the type name at registration, other SDKs at definition.

Source claim (112-119): arguments and return values must be serializable; writes should be idempotent; Activities have timeouts and retry policies and should either complete within a few minutes or heartbeat; at least one timeout, typically start_to_close, is required, and a shorter timeout detects and retries problems sooner.

Representation note: the page has no diagrams or tables; it is prose, bullet lists, callouts and one Go code sample. Linked per-SDK how-to pages, retry-policy encyclopedia entries and the Standalone Activity page are outside this unit.

sections: Worker Deployments: logical service grouped for unified management (15-17)
Worker Deployment Versions: deployment name plus Build ID, shared build and environment (19-21)
Versioning behaviors: Pinned; Auto-Upgrade; Activity behavior across versions and Independent Activities (23-54)
Versioning Definitions: Current, Ramping and Target Worker Deployment Version (56-60)
Versioning statuses: Inactive, Active, Draining and Drained (62-69)
Continue-as-new, Child Workflow, and Retry Semantics: ways new runs start; inheritance overview; child workflow, continue-as-new, retry and cron scenarios; Versioning Override inheritance (71-140)
notes: Source claim (15-21): a Worker Deployment is a logical service grouping similar Workers for unified management, with a name and a series of Deployment Versions; each version is identified by deployment name plus Build ID, groups Workers that share code build and environment, and reports itself to the Temporal Server when polling.

Source claim (25-35): each Workflow Type can declare Pinned or Auto-Upgrade behavior. Pinned is guaranteed to complete on one Deployment Version and can be moved only with `temporal workflow update-options`; Auto-Upgrade moves to the latest version when the current version changes and must be kept replay-safe manually with patching.

Inference: Pinned removes replay exposure at the cost of leaving old Workers polling; Auto-Upgrade removes old-version residue at the cost of a permanent patching obligation. The page states both mechanisms but does not compare their operational costs.

Source claim (37-54): Activities generally start on their Workflow's version, the pinned version for Pinned workflows or the Target version for Auto-Upgrade workflows, moving the execution immediately before the Activity if needed. Independent Activities are the exception and start on their own Task Queue's Current or Ramping version; examples include a separate deployment, an unversioned queue, or a shared Activity from another deployment.

Source claim (56-60): Current is the default route for new and non-pinned work; other versions keep polling for pinned workflows and rollback. Ramping routes a configurable percentage [0,100] by Workflow ID, with the remainder on Current. Target is the next version, Current or Ramping; a 5% ramp to C gives each Workflow roughly a 5% chance of Target C based on its ID.

Source claim (62-69): version states are Inactive (exists only because a Worker polled), Active (Current or Ramping), Draining (open pinned workflows remain after loss of Current or Ramping), and Drained (all pinned workflows closed). Drained is not absolute: closed workflows can re-run code paths if queried within retention while Workers of that version still poll.

Source claim (71-105): new runs arise from Child Workflows, Continue-As-New, Retry Policy and Cron. Auto-Upgrade workflows never inherit versions; Pinned workflows pass their version to pinned children when the child's Task Queue belongs to that version. A Pinned parent's child first task runs in the parent's version; a Pinned child stays pinned, an Auto-Upgrade child changes behavior after the first task, and a child in a different Worker Deployment starts on that queue's Current version.

Source claim (107-132): a Pinned version crosses Continue-As-New runs unless the new run's Task Queue is outside the Worker Deployment; Auto-Upgrade does not inherit. Retry inheritance requires all three conditions: effectively pinned at retry time, inherited a pinned version at start, and running on a Task Queue in that version; otherwise no inheritance. Cron jobs never inherit versioning behavior or version.

Source claim (134-140): children, crons, retries and Continue-As-New inherit the source run's Versioning Override if the override is pinned and the new Workflow's Task Queue belongs to the override version; override inheritance is evaluated separately and takes precedence over the inherited base version.

Inference: inheritance is decided by Task Queue membership in the Worker Deployment, not by Workflow ID or parent-child relation alone; an inherited version that the queue does not serve falls back to Current. This makes deployment topology part of workflow semantics.

Inference: the page is a concept reference, not an implementation guide. It names SDK or CLI declaration and `update-options`, but gives no code, no default for undeclared Workflow Types, no retention or deployment limits, and no rollback procedure. The linked production Worker Versioning page and CLI reference are outside this unit.

tycho_candidates.candidate: The page says old histories need a compatible worker route and that worker-version routing is not prescribed (118-122, 142); the source supplies Pinned versus Auto-Upgrade, Deployment Versions and Draining/Drained states (25-35, 62-69). Add the explicit route while keeping the page's caution that versioning does not prove external effects exactly once.

The page frames compatibility as old/new caller and server pairs (49-64); the source adds a third dimension: a Pinned workflow stays on an old Worker version while an Auto-Upgrade workflow moves. Use it to distinguish protocol compatibility from execution-history compatibility.

The source's Ramping percentage routes Workflows by Workflow ID, not a percentage of traffic, and rollback means changing Current or Ramping while pinned workflows drain (56-69); contrast this with the page's warning that a traffic percentage does not bound old-reader exposure (73, 84), without equating the two mechanisms.

The source makes version inheritance a property of workflow chains (children, Continue-As-New, retries, cron; 71-140), while the page treats durable-coordinator guarantees as conditional on versioned workflow-state persistence and activity semantics (81-89, 105). Add chain-level inheritance as a concrete case.

The page's mixed-version reader/writer matrix covers data compatibility (51-67); the source's Active/Draining/Drained states are an analogous coexistence window for code. Use it to show why retiring an old Worker version requires proving no pinned workflows remain, not merely that no new traffic arrives.

Source claim (3-5): Core NATS delivers only to subscribers connected at publication time, is at-most-once and never replayed; JetStream adds a persistence layer giving at-least-once delivery, survival across restarts and replay, and extends decoupling from identity to time.

Source claim (23, Streams): a stream binds to one or more subject patterns; a published message matching a pattern is appended and assigned a sequence number; streams are configurable for storage (memory or disk), retention (limits or consumer acks), replication 'and more'. Source claim (27): a consumer is a server-side, stateful view that tracks client progress; multiple consumers read the same stream independently, each with its own position, and the server maintains that position so applications need not coordinate it.

Source claim (29): a second animated figure describes three consumers with independent cursors over an 8-message stream, starting at different points and never moving each other's position, served from one shared copy. Caption only; no numbers beyond the caption are given.

Source claim (31-33): an acknowledgement advances the consumer cursor; a message not acknowledged in time is redelivered, 'which is what gives you at-least-once delivery'; a consumer can start at the beginning, at the latest message, at a sequence number or at a time. Source claim (37-65 and the seven other client sections): the CLI and client samples perform one scenario - add stream ORDERS (file storage, limits retention), publish three orders, add a durable pull consumer with explicit ack and deliver-all, fetch three and acknowledge. [source] V1.1.1 requires untrusted input to be decoded or unescaped into canonical form exactly once, only when encoded data in that form is expected, and before further processing; V1.1.2 requires output encoding/escaping as a final step before the interpreter, or by the interpreter itself.

[source] V1.2.10 addresses CSV and formula injection: RFC 4180 sections 2.6-2.7 escaping for CSV, and a leading single quote for '=', '+', '-', '@', tab and null when exporting to CSV or spreadsheet formats.
[source] The V1.2 note states that parameterized queries or SQL escaping are not always sufficient because identifiers such as table, column and ORDER BY names cannot be escaped.

[source] V1.5.3 requires different parsers for the same data type (JSON, XML, URL) to parse consistently and use the same character encoding, citing JSON interoperability, RFI and SSRF as consequences of divergent parsing.

[source] V2.2.2 requires input validation to be enforced at a trusted service layer and states that client-side validation must not be relied on as a security control; schema validation is described as effective but not mandated.

[source] V2.3 covers step order, documented business limits, business-level transactions/rollback, locking against double-booking, and multi-user approval for high-value flows; V2.4 covers anti-automation and realistic human timing.

[source] V3 requires cookie prefixes and attributes, HSTS with at least one year and preload, CSP with object-src/base-uri 'none' and either an allowlist or nonces/hashes (per-response nonces or hashes at L3), nosniff, referrer policy, frame-ancestors, COOP, SRI for external assets, restricted redirects, and rejection of untrusted postMessage origins.

[source] V4 requires content-type/charset correctness, non-overridable intermediary headers, HTTP method allowlists, request-smuggling-resistant framing (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding and HTTP/2-3 DATA frames), CR/LF rejection, GraphQL cost/introspection controls, and WSS plus Origin checks and HTTPS-derived session tokens for WebSocket.

[source] V5 requires documented file types/sizes, size and magic-byte/content checks, archive expansion limits, per-user quotas, rejection of symlinks and pixel floods, non-executable public storage, trusted path construction, zip-slip protection, safe download filenames (RFC 6266) and antivirus scanning.

[inference] The chapters state verification requirements and control objectives, not architecture mechanisms or evidence that any system satisfies them; mapping to Tycho pages is a parent task, and no support, severity or acceptance judgment is offered here.

notes.text: Defines 'happened before' (arrow) as the smallest relation closed under same-process order, message send-before-receipt and transitivity; events with neither a->b nor b->a are concurrent (lines 113-125).

The Clock Condition (a->b implies C(a)<C(b), not the converse) follows from C1 (same-process monotonicity) and C2 (send precedes receipt), realised by IR1 (increment between events) and IR2 (timestamp messages; receiver advances past Tm) (lines 176-194).

Any clock system satisfying the Clock Condition yields a total order by comparing (Ci(a), process id) lexicographically; the order extends the partial order, is not unique, and different clocks give different total orders (lines 209-226).

Mutual exclusion is solved with timestamped request/acknowledgement/release messages and per-process request queues: a process may use the resource when its own request is ordered first in its queue and it has received a later-timestamped message from every other process; the algorithm has no central process or storage (lines 232-290).

The total order supports replicated state machines: each process executes commands in timestamp order once it knows all commands with smaller timestamps; because every process must participate, failure of one process halts progress (lines 291-325).

Anomalous behavior occurs when the algorithm's order contradicts an order users perceive through channels outside the system (telephone example); remedies are to inject external precedence into timestamps or to use physical clocks meeting the Strong Clock Condition (lines 277-320).

Physical clocks must satisfy PC1 (rate error below kappa, kappa about 1e-6 for crystal clocks) and PC2 (mutual skew below epsilon), and are only ever reset forward; IR1'/IR2' reset to max(local clock, Tm + minimum delay) (lines 349-372, 423-427).

Theorem: for a strongly connected graph of diameter d where a message with unpredictable delay at most xi crosses every arc within tau seconds, PC2 holds with epsilon = d(2*kappa*tau + xi) for t > t0 + tau*d; the Appendix proves it via inequalities (1)-(12) (lines 411-431, 473-538).
Anomalous behavior is impossible if epsilon/(1-kappa) <= mu, where mu is a lower bound on interprocess transmission time (lines 428-433).
The author argues failure is meaningful only relative to physical time, calls failure handling out of scope, and points to a separate method for tolerating process and link failure (lines 321-334).

Read as architecture guidance, the paper establishes causal ordering and deterministic command sequencing only; it contains no leader election, quorum commitment or crash-recovery protocol, so treating it as a consensus algorithm would overstate the source (inference from lines 232-334).

notes.text: Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, safety and membership change, and enforces a strong leader so log entries flow only from leader to followers (lines 57-71, 154-173).

Terms are consecutive integers that act as a logical clock: currentTerm increases monotonically, at most one leader exists per term, and any RPC carrying a higher term forces a server to adopt it and revert to follower (lines 286-325).

Leader election uses randomized timeouts from a fixed interval (for example 150-300 ms) to make split votes rare; a candidate needs a majority, and RequestVote carries lastLogIndex/lastLogTerm so voters reject candidates whose logs are less up to date (lines 189-253, 325-374, 484-503).

Log Matching (equal index and term imply identical prefixes) is enforced by the AppendEntries prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm consistency check with an induction argument; a leader repairs a follower by decrementing nextIndex and retrying (lines 376-446).

Only entries from the leader's current term are committed by counting replicas; committing one such entry commits all preceding entries indirectly, and a leader must not infer commitment of a previous-term entry from replica counts alone (Figure 8) (lines 399-417, 532-560).
Five properties are stated to hold at all times: Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety (lines 259-273).

The safety argument proves Leader Completeness by contradiction using a voter in the intersection of the electing majority and the committing majority, then derives State Machine Safety and identical application order (lines 561-580).
Timing requirement: broadcastTime much less than electionTimeout much less than MTBF; safety must not depend on timing, while availability inevitably does (lines 599-637).

Membership changes use joint consensus C_old,new requiring separate majorities of both configurations; new servers join first as non-voting members, and removed servers are neutralised by ignoring RequestVote within the minimum election timeout of hearing from a leader (lines 603-696).

Log compaction uses snapshots recording lastIncludedIndex, lastIncludedTerm and the latest configuration; InstallSnapshot streams chunks, and a follower receiving a prefix snapshot deletes covered entries but keeps later ones (lines 686-799, 699-736).

Client interaction: linearizable semantics are obtained with per-client serial numbers and cached responses to suppress duplicate execution; read-only requests require a committed no-op from the leader's term and a heartbeat majority check (lines 765-779, 800-818).

The user study (43 participants, mean 25.7 vs 20.8 out of 60, 4.9-point difference, 33 of 41 self-reports favoring Raft) measures learnability of two lecture-and-quiz presentations prepared by the authors, not runtime behavior or independent adoption (inference from lines 810-892).

notes.text: Safety requirements are stated as: only a proposed value may be chosen, only a single value is chosen, and a process learns a value only if it has actually been chosen; liveness is deliberately not specified precisely (lines 44-53).
Model is asynchronous and non-Byzantine: agents run at arbitrary speed, may stop and restart, messages may take arbitrarily long, be duplicated or lost, but are not corrupted (lines 59-70).

Majorities intersect, so a single value per acceptor would suffice in the absence of failure, but P1 (accept the first proposal) plus majority choice forces acceptors to accept multiple numbered proposals (lines 77-110).

Safety is reduced in steps from P2 to P2a to P2b to the invariant P2c, which a proposer maintains by learning the highest-numbered proposal accepted in some majority and by extracting a promise not to accept lower-numbered proposals (lines 111-166).

The algorithm runs in two phases: prepare (promise plus highest accepted proposal) and accept (value fixed by the highest-numbered response, or free if none); acceptors keep the highest accepted proposal and highest promised prepare in stable storage across restarts (lines 167-244, 219-225, 323-326).

Learning options are acceptors replying to every learner (acceptors x learners messages), a distinguished learner (sum of acceptors and learners), or a set of distinguished learners trading reliability against message count (lines 257-287).

Progress requires a distinguished proposer; two proposers can keep raising proposal numbers and starve each other, and the FLP result implies leader election must use randomness or real time, while safety holds regardless of election success (lines 289-311).

In the implementation each process plays all roles, one leader acts as distinguished proposer and learner, proposal numbers come from disjoint per-proposer sets, and acceptors record intended responses before sending them (lines 313-333).

The state machine is a sequence of consensus instances where the i-th chosen value is the i-th command; a leader that gets alpha commands ahead can leave a gap of up to alpha-1, filled with no-op commands, and phase 1 over infinitely many instances costs one short message (lines 336-431).

Reconfiguration is itself a state-machine decision: the set of servers implementing instance i+alpha is determined by the state after the i-th command, permitting arbitrary reconfiguration policies (lines 451-459).

The text is a derivation and specification, not an evaluation: it reports no measurements, implementation or failure-injection results, so it cannot evidence performance or operational behavior (inference from the whole document, especially lines 374-438).

notes: [claim] Dynamo is presented as a highly available key-value store for Amazon's platform that sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios and relies on object versioning plus application-assisted conflict resolution (lines 32-45).

[claim] The design synthesizes consistent hashing, vector clocks, a quorum-like replica synchronization protocol, and gossip-based membership/failure detection, with no central administration (lines 73-90).
[claim] The target is an 'always writeable' store: writes must not be rejected under failures, so conflict resolution complexity is pushed to reads (lines 207-236).

[claim] Reads and writes use a 'sloppy quorum' over the first N healthy nodes in the preference list, with hinted handoff for temporary failures and read repair for stale replicas (lines 500-510, 512-534, 670-675).
[claim] Anti-entropy uses Merkle trees, one per key range, to synchronize divergent replicas in the background (lines 500-535).

[claim] A typical production configuration is N=3 and (N,R,W)=(3,2,2); service SLAs are stated at the 99.9th percentile, and Dynamo targets 99.9% of requests within 300 ms (lines 696-697, 745-748, 764-768).
[claim] Reported production outcomes: 99.9995% of requests received successful responses and no data-loss event 'to date'; 99.94% of requests saw exactly one version (lines 873-875, 959-963).
[claim] Client-driven request coordination reduced 99.9th-percentile read/write latency from 68.9/68.5 ms to 30.4/30.4 ms in a 24-hour comparison (Table 2, lines 927-939).
[claim] The full-membership gossip model works at 'couple of hundreds of nodes' but is not trivially scalable to tens of thousands; hierarchical or O(1) DHT extensions are suggested (lines 992-1003).

[claim] Dynamo assumes a trusted, non-hostile environment with no authentication/authorization, targets objects usually under 1 MB, and is used within a single administrative domain (lines 106, 131-135, 329-332).

[inference] The operational percentages are operator-reported aggregates without raw distributions, so they document a deployment experience rather than a reproducible measurement; they should be cited as vendor claims.

[inference] The paper reports techniques and production lessons, not a head-to-head benchmark; latency numbers depend on the reported (3,2,2) configuration and hardware, so cross-system comparison is not supported by this text alone.

notes: [claim] Spanner is described as a scalable, multi-version, globally distributed, synchronously replicated database and the first system to distribute data at global scale while supporting externally consistent distributed transactions (lines 13-24, 62-67).

[claim] Data is sharded across Paxos state machines in datacenters; zones are the unit of administrative deployment and physical isolation, and a Spanner deployment is called a universe (lines 28-40, 100-110, 123-126).

[claim] TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty as a TTinterval; implementations use GPS and atomic clocks, with epsilon typically under 10 ms, a 1-7 ms sawtooth over a 30-second poll interval, and about 4 ms most of the time (lines 68-77, 260-283, 296-304).

[claim] Commit wait delays visibility of a commit until TT.after(s) holds, ensuring the assigned timestamp precedes the absolute commit time; the expected wait is at least 2*epsilon (lines 412-423, 500-507).

[claim] Read-only transactions are lock-free and execute at a chosen timestamp; replicas serve reads only when their safe time covers the read timestamp, with tsafe = min(tPaxos_safe, tTM_safe) (lines 337-352, 441-445).
[claim] Paxos leaders hold time-based leases (10 s default) with a disjointness invariant that supports monotonically increasing timestamps across leaders (lines 136-141, 315-330, 350-370).

[claim] Microbenchmarks on timeshared 4-core machines: one-replica write latency 9.4+/-0.6 ms with commit wait disabled, 14.4+/-1.0 ms at 1 replica with commit wait; snapshot-read throughput reaches 50.0+/-1.1 Kops/s at 5 replicas (Table 3, lines 515-522).
[claim] Two-phase commit remains reasonable to about 50 participants; mean latency rises from 17.0 ms at 1 participant to 42.7 ms at 50 and 150.5 ms at 200 (Table 4, lines 579-597, 616-621).

[claim] In the availability experiment, killing a non-leader zone had no visible effect (about 3-4% throughput loss), while killing the leader zone dropped completion nearly to zero until leaders were re-elected, with recovery around the 10-second lease horizon (lines 625-641, 655-660).
[claim] F1-perceived latencies over 24 hours: all reads mean 8.7 ms, single-site commit 72.3 ms, multi-site commit 103.0 ms, with large standard deviations (Table 6, lines 715-742).
[claim] Schema-change transactions are assigned a future timestamp and proceed without blocking unrelated reads/writes, relying on TrueTime to make 'at time t' meaningful (lines 491-511).

[inference] 'First system' and global-scale claims are the authors' characterization of Google's deployment; the paper reports no independent reproduction, and the design target of millions of machines and trillions of rows (lines 39-40) is not evidence of deployed scale.

[source claim] The master holds per-task state (idle, in-progress, completed) plus worker identity, and for each completed map task the locations and sizes of its R intermediate file regions, pushed incrementally to workers with in-progress reduce tasks; scheduling state is O(M+R) and per-pair state about one byte (L195-210, L280-291).

[inference] The availability argument therefore covers worker failure only; the paper gives no master-failure rate or failover measurement, so single-master abort is a stated design trade rather than an evaluated one.

[source claim] Locality uses 64 MB input blocks with typically three replicas: a map task is scheduled on a machine holding a replica, otherwise near one (L261-280).

notes: [source claim] HNSW is a fully graph-based K-ANNS index needing no auxiliary coarse-search structure; it builds a multi-layer proximity graph over nested subsets, and each element's top layer is l = floor(-ln(unif(0,1)) * mL), an exponentially decaying level distribution (L11-22, L243-270).

[source claim] Insertion (Alg. 1) greedily descends from the top layer with ef=1, then from min(L,l) to layer 0 uses efConstruction, connects the new element to M selected neighbours, and shrinks any neighbour's list above Mmax (Mmax0 at layer 0) (L243-270).

[source claim] Search (Alg. 5) uses ef=1 above layer 0 and a dynamic candidate list of size ef at layer 0; the layer search (Alg. 2) stops when the nearest candidate is farther than the furthest result, not after a fixed number of distance computations (L249-300).

[source claim] The neighbour heuristic (Alg. 4) keeps a candidate only if it is closer to the base element than any already selected neighbour; given enough candidates it yields the exact relative neighbourhood graph as a subgraph, and in 1D the exact Delaunay subgraph, which is the stated correspondence to a skip list (L207-241, L275-305).

[source claim] Recommended settings are mL = 1/ln(M) (skip-list p=1/M), Mmax0 = 2*M, M in 5-48 (6-48 in the memory section), and efConstruction = 100 for a reasonable index; setting Mmax0 = M is reported to penalise high-recall search (L306-350, L433-460, L611-626).

[source claim] Under an assumption of exact Delaunay graphs the expected steps per layer are bounded by S = 1/(1-exp(-mL)), independent of dataset size, giving O(log N) search and O(N log N) construction; the authors acknowledge the assumption is violated by approximate selection and rely on zero-layer backtracking, with simulations said to show unchanged scaling (L563-606).
[source claim] Memory per element is (Mmax0 + mL*Mmax) * bytes_per_link; with four-byte links and M in 6-48 this is about 60-450 bytes per object excluding the stored data (L611-626).

[source claim] Evaluation is single-threaded on a 4x Xeon E5-4650 v2, 128 GB RAM, GCC 5.3 with -Ofast, using ann-benchmark with 1,000 queries per dataset; baselines are NSW, FLANN, Annoy, VP-tree, FALCONN and Faiss PQ (L629-750, L911-936).

[source claim] Build cost: on a 200M SIFT subset HNSW is reported at 5.6 h and 64 GB peak with efConstruction=500, or 42 min with efConstruction=40, versus Faiss at 11-12 h and 23.5-30 GB; on 10M SIFT, efConstruction=100 builds in about 3 minutes on a 4x 2.4 GHz 10-core server, and construction parallelises with few synchronisation points and no measurable index-quality effect (Table 3, Fig. 15, L548-560, L864-936).

[source claim] Stated limitation: the fixed top-layer entry point prevents NSW-style distributed search because of higher-layer congestion; partitioning data across nodes is possible but total parallel throughput is said not to scale well, and skip-list-like distribution is left as a possibility (L923-943).

[inference] The headline comparisons are per-dataset query-time/recall curves from one machine generation and one query batch; the text reports no tail latency, concurrent-query throughput, filtered search, or supported update/delete path, and the Discussion lists element updates and removal as future work (L985-990), so those properties are outside what this unit demonstrates.

[inference] The vector-space comparison selects each baseline's best result within every recall range (L735-742), which works against HNSW; the reported lead is therefore unlikely to be an artefact of weak baseline tuning, though the margins remain specific to these datasets, parameter sweeps and one machine.

notes.text: The OAS is defined as a language-agnostic interface description for HTTP APIs; an OpenAPI Description may be distributed across multiple documents, all of which MUST be complete documents with an OpenAPI or Schema Object root and MUST be fully parsed before any reference is treated as unresolvable.

Versions use major.minor.patch; patch releases only address errors or clarifications, tooling SHOULD be compatible across patch levels, and minor versions may include non-backwards-compatible changes. The document distinguishes undefined behavior (may contradict the spec; NOT RECOMMENDED to rely on) from implementation-defined behavior (safe only when all relevant tools agree).

The root OpenAPI Object requires openapi and info and at least one of components, paths, or webhooks; $self gives the document's self-assigned URI and base URI. Server url supports variables and may be relative; relative API URLs resolve against Server URLs rather than the document's $self.

Parameter locations are path, query, querystring, header, cookie; query and querystring parameters MUST NOT coexist in one operation or its path item, and querystring parameters require content. The style table permits matrix/label/simple/form/spaceDelimited/pipeDelimited/deepObject/cookie combinations; cookie style applies no percent-encoding.

Media Type Objects add itemSchema, prefixEncoding, and itemEncoding for sequential and streaming content; sequential media types MUST be mapped to the JSON Schema data model as arrays, and text/event-stream data MUST be parsed per the HTML event-stream rules, with unknown fields and comments ignored.

application/x-www-form-urlencoded content MUST be percent-encoded per WHATWG-URL rules after complex values are serialized; multipart contentType defaults depend on schema type and contentEncoding, and media-type sniffing MUST NOT be the default when multiple content types are allowed.

Example Object dataValue MUST be valid against its schema; serializedValue and externalValue MUST show the serialized form; value is deprecated for non-JSON serialization targets. Validation of serialized examples is explicitly best-effort because some formats admit multiple valid representations and parsing can be ambiguous.

Runtime expressions follow an ABNF grammar over $url, $method, $statusCode, $request.<source>, and $response.<source>, where source is a header, query, path, or body reference and body references use RFC6901 JSON Pointers.

The Schema Object is a superset of JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 plus the OAS base vocabulary, with a default dialect URI of the form https://spec.openapis.org/oas/3.2/dialect/YYYY-MM-DD. Discriminator is legal only with oneOf, anyOf, or allOf, MUST NOT change validation outcomes, and when the discriminating property is optional a defaultMapping is mandatory.

Security Scheme types are apiKey, http, mutualTLS, oauth2, openIdConnect. Security Requirement names that equal a Components name are treated as component names before URI resolution; the specification itself calls the resulting ambiguity exploitable and says naming a component like a URI is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The local representation omits the entire body of section 4.21 Header Object; the TOC lists four subsections, but the text jumps from the runtime-expression table to the Tag Object. Header field semantics, link-header modeling, Set-Cookie representation, and the header example cannot be cited from this file. The gap is in the representation, not necessarily in the published standard.

The five book candidates are selected only for topical adjacency to interface descriptions, versioning, API contract layers, and service descriptions. This record makes no support, severity, acceptance, or comparison judgment; candidate mapping and any baseline anchoring remain with the parent.

notes.text: The document header declares CloudEvents Version 1.0.3-wip. The specversion attribute must be the string '1.0' for this version, and patch-level changes are not reflected in specversion (lines 1, 335-351).

REQUIRED context attributes are id, source, specversion and type. Producers MUST ensure source+id is unique per distinct event; a re-sent duplicate MAY keep the same id, and consumers MAY treat identical source+id as duplicates (lines 282-370).
OPTIONAL core attributes are datacontenttype, dataschema, subject and time. Extension attributes MAY be added provided they follow the same naming convention and type system (lines 372-507).

Attribute names are restricted to lowercase ASCII a-z and 0-9, SHOULD start with a letter, SHOULD NOT exceed 20 characters, and MUST NOT be 'data'. Values use Boolean, Integer (signed 32-bit), String, Binary, URI, URI-reference or Timestamp (lines 187-248).
Intermediaries MUST forward events of 64 KiB or less and consumers SHOULD accept at least 64 KiB. Size is wire-size, including protocol frame metadata, event metadata and data (lines 549-574).

All implementations MUST support the JSON event format. Every event format MUST define a structured-mode representation and MAY define batch mode; all events in one batch MUST share the same specversion (lines 32-35, 127-154).
Privacy guidance says sensitive information SHOULD NOT be carried in context attributes, event data SHOULD be encrypted, and protocol-level security SHOULD be employed (lines 584-611).

CloudEvents is an event-format and interoperability specification; it does not define delivery guarantees, retry policy, ordering or exactly-once processing. Those claims would need a separate source.
Because source+id uniqueness is scoped to a producer/source, the duplicate assumption is local to that scope; global deduplication needs additional identity beyond CloudEvents.
The 64 KiB rule is a forwarding floor, not an end-to-end size guarantee: larger events are permitted where intermediaries and consumers accept them.
dataschema identifies a schema by URI but the specification imposes no schema language, validation algorithm or compatibility test.

Manifest entry R141 has an empty url and title. Batch file /tmp/B19/raw/urls.txt records https://github.com/cloudevents/spec, and the document header supplies the 1.0.3-wip title. This is a manifest metadata omission, not a representation gap and not a different edition.

notes.text: Trace context is split into traceparent, a fixed-length portable position in the trace graph, and tracestate, optional vendor-specific name/value pairs. Every tracing tool MUST set traceparent even when relying only on tracestate (lines 130-135).
Minimum compliant behavior is forwarding both headers without breaking traces; a tool may additionally participate by modifying traceparent and its own tracestate portion (lines 137-142).
If a tracestate header arrives without traceparent, it is invalid and MUST be discarded (lines 156-160).

On an outgoing request the vendor MUST update parent-id to the current operation and MAY set the sampled flag; modified or new tracestate keys MUST move to the beginning of the list, and vendors SHOULD NOT delete keys they did not generate (lines 175-187).

Privacy rules forbid personally identifiable or sensitive information in traceparent/tracestate; random number generators MUST NOT rely on user-identifiable information, and tracestate MUST NOT include PII (lines 199-221).

trace-id SHOULD be globally unique and randomly generated. Shorter internal identifiers SHOULD be left-padded with zeros when generating a 16-byte trace-id, and the rightmost part SHOULD be used when receiving (lines 251-282).

notes.text: Baggage standardizes representation and propagation of application-defined properties associated with a distributed request or workflow execution, independent of Trace Context (lines 8-12).
The current version targets applications and services, including browser applications; web browsers or user agents are not currently in scope as a target implementation (line 14).

The document is a Candidate Recommendation Snapshot under the 2023 W3C Process and is not expected to advance to Proposed Recommendation earlier than 30 August 2024. The CR stage plans an audit of OpenTelemetry baggage implementations and a sample of its test suites (lines 20-29).

Libraries and platforms SHOULD propagate the baggage header, and systems MUST assess the risk of header abuse; proprietary information should not be stored in baggage or should not cross trust boundaries (lines 75, 79, 85).

notes: Source claim (L14-22): this is R2DBC 1.0.0.RELEASE, status Final, released 2022-04-25 under Apache License 2.0. Inference: the revision is fixed by this representation; later R2DBC editions are outside this unit.

Source claim (L76-94): R2DBC is an SPI for JVM languages giving reactive access to SQL/tabular data sources, built on Reactive Streams Publisher/Subscriber with non-blocking back-pressure, a Java 8 baseline, non-null semantics by default and zero-based parameter/column indexes. Inference: the specification assumes a reactive runtime and does not itself schedule work.

Source claim (L322-384): compliance requires non-blocking I/O, ServiceLoader discovery of ConnectionFactoryProvider, and full implementation of ConnectionFactory, ConnectionFactoryMetadata, ConnectionFactoryProvider, Result, Row, RowMetadata and Batch; listed Connection/Statement/ColumnMetadata methods are optional with defined fallbacks. Inference: a compliant driver may still lack savepoints, generated keys, fetch-size hints or full column metadata.

Source claim (L404-526): connection URLs use scheme r2dbc or r2dbcs, a driver identifier, optional protocol, authority (possibly multiple hosts), path and query; the fragment is reserved; URL parts map to SSL/DRIVER/PROTOCOL/USER/PASSWORD/HOST/PORT/DATABASE, and parsed extended options are Strings because of type erasure. Inference: URL configuration is lossy with respect to Option<T> types.

Source claim (L589-595): ConnectionFactory creation is deferred until Subscription.request(1), must emit exactly one Connection or an error, must be cancellable with resource release, and wrappers must implement Wrapped<ConnectionFactory>. Inference: connection acquisition is itself a reactive resource lifecycle, not a blocking factory call.

Source claim (L768-784, L816-826): transactions are mandatory; auto-commit is the default for new connections; beginTransaction disables it; the isolation default is vendor-specific and setting isolation during a transaction is vendor-specific. Inference: portable guarantees cover transaction boundaries more than isolation semantics.

Source claim (L893-901): drivers without savepoint support should throw UnsupportedOperationException for createSavepoint and rollbackTransactionToSavepoint, while releaseSavepoint is a no-op; savepoints end with commit or rollback. Inference: savepoint support is optional and observable only through documented method behavior.

Source claim (L956-989, L1035-1071): binding accepts a zero-based index or a placeholder, with scalar values or Parameter/Type objects; execute throws IllegalStateException if any marker lacks a binding; IN, IN/OUT and OUT parameters are supported. Inference: statement validity depends on complete binding sets, not SQL parsing alone.

Source claim (L1145-1164, L1194): Result is forward-only and read-only and may expose rows, OUT parameters or an update count, but not both through the same consumption path; Row is valid only inside the mapping callback. Inference: consumers cannot retain rows or freely mix result modes across drivers.

Source claim (L1369, L1433): ColumnMetadata and OutParameterMetadata must expose metadata available as a by-product of execution but cannot issue queries because their methods are expected to be non-blocking; some methods are optional. Inference: metadata completeness is best-effort and vendor-dependent.

Source claim (L1503-1549): R2dbcException carries message, SQLState, error code, SQL text and cause; non-transient and transient hierarchies map common states to named subclasses. Inference: portable retry classification can key on transient versus non-transient categories rather than SQLState text.

Source claim (L1687-1700, L1716-1817): Blob/Clob streams follow Reactive Streams, can be consumed only once, remain valid at least for the transaction and are released by consumption or discard(); Wrapped, Closeable and Lifecycle are optional extensions, with postAllocate/preRelease called around pooled use. Inference: LOB and pooled-connection resource safety depends on subscriber behavior rather than garbage collection.

notes.text: OpenGitOps describes itself as a set of open-source standards, best practices and community-focused education for a structured, standardized approach to GitOps (lines 8-10).
The page labels the principles v1.0.0 and lists four: Declarative, Versioned and Immutable, Pulled Automatically, Continuously Reconciled (lines 27-51).
Declarative: a system managed by GitOps must have its desired state expressed declaratively (lines 31-33).
Versioned and Immutable: desired state is stored in a way that enforces immutability, versioning and retains a complete version history (lines 37-39).
Pulled Automatically: software agents automatically pull desired state declarations from the source (lines 43-45).
Continuously Reconciled: software agents continuously observe actual system state and attempt to apply the desired state (lines 49-51).

The page carries three practitioner testimonial quotes and a footer attributing the site to OpenGitOps, the GitOps Working Group and the Linux Foundation, with a 2026 copyright line (lines 12-25, 55-56).
The four principles constrain the delivery model rather than prescribe an architecture; repository layout, controller choice, sync tooling and promotion mechanics are unspecified on this page.
Automatic pulling implies agents need read access to the source and write access to the target, but the page says nothing about credentials, trust boundaries or isolation.
No conformance criteria, maturity levels, audit procedure or exception handling appear on the landing page; 'principles' here are directional requirements, not a testable standard.
The linked glossary and v1.0.0 document define the terms operationally; without them, terms such as 'declarative', 'state store' and 'reconciliation' are only glossed by the one-line principles.
The 'Published Time: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 13:04:40 GMT' header is a server/fetch timestamp, not a GitOps Principles revision date; the principles version is the explicit v1.0.0 label.
